lotrim construction, inc., represented by its president, engineer odilon marlon l. gaviola, and engineer odilon marlon l. gaviola, petitioners, vs. commission on audit, respondent. vii. constitutional commissions > b. civil service commission (csc), commission on elections (comelec), and commission on audit (coa) > 2. powers, functions, and jurisdiction **coa proper is not limited to the grounds relied upon by the auditor** (*yap v. coa*, reiterated). in the exercise of its constitutional audit power (const., art. ix-d, sec. 2(2)), it must make its own assessment of a disallowance. it may adjust the amount, identify additional persons liable, or modify their participation without a separate audit observation memorandum, notice of suspension or notice of disallowance, provided the parties have a fair opportunity to be heard. due process is satisfied where the party could explain its side or seek reconsideration. coa's technical and information technology services (techits) is an internal office answerable only to coa, so it need not notify the contractor of its inspection or furnish it its report.

**quantum meruit cuts both ways.** it lets a contractor recover the reasonable value of work done under a void government contract. but it "cannot be distorted into a shield for contractors to retain payments in excess of what is legally or contractually due": the government may recover payments that exceed the actual accomplishment. coa's factual findings on the amount due, if supported by substantial evidence, are respected.

procedurally, under **rule 64, sec. 3**, the petition must be filed within 30 days from notice. a motion for reconsideration interrupts the period, and after its denial only the remaining period, but not less than five days, is left. a late petition makes the coa ruling final and immutable. also, **a party who actively participated in the coa proceedings and sought affirmative relief is estopped from belatedly invoking ciac jurisdiction** under an arbitration clause (*tijam v. sibonghanoy*; *amoguis v. ballado*). v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64) ii. jurisdiction > b. subject matter jurisdiction > 2. effect of estoppel
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-249759-20260422:
juanito b. soto, petitioner, vs. cassandra reyes-soto and the republic of the philippines, respondents. iii. family relations > a. marriage (const., art. ii, sec. 12, and art. xv) > 4. void and voidable marriages whether the evidence proves psychological incapacity, including the credibility and weight of expert testimony, is a **question of fact** that is not proper in a rule 45 petition; the rtc's findings, affirmed by the ca, bind the supreme court absent a recognized exception. ruling on the merits anyway, the court **reiterated tan-andal v. andal, georfo v. republic and estella v. perez**: psychological incapacity under article 36 of the family code is a legal, not a medical, concept and must be proved by **clear and convincing evidence**. three requisites must concur: (1) **juridical antecedence**, meaning it existed when the marriage was celebrated even if it showed only later; (2) **incurability in the legal sense**, meaning a condition so enduring and persistent with respect to the specific spouse that the marriage is beyond repair; and (3) **gravity**, meaning a genuinely psychic cause, not mere refusal, neglect, difficulty or ill will. expert opinion is not required. ordinary witnesses and the offended spouse may testify to the dysfunctional acts.

**clarified on expert evidence:** when offered, expert testimony is an aid, not a controlling determinant. it must link observed behavior and life history to antecedence, incurability and gravity, and its weight depends on the expert's qualifications, sound methodology, and whether it rests on hearsay (halog v. halog). **no rule requires the expert to personally interview both spouses.** doing so is ideal but not indispensable. a psychiatrist's testimony does not lose probative value because another person administered the psychological tests, if she interpreted and integrated the results and they only corroborated her own interview-based findings. **"silent dysfunction"** (emotional distance, withdrawal and resignation) may amount to psychological incapacity even without violence or infidelity, and both spouses may be declared incapacitated.

property relations in a void marriage are governed by article 147 or 148 of the family code. under article 147 the properties are co-owned and may be partitioned by agreement or by judicial proceedings (civil code, art. 496), so **partition is only incidental to the declaration of nullity and is not a prerequisite for it** (diño v. diño, reiterated). iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > e. modes > v. appeal by certiorari to sc (rule 45) viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 3. testimonial evidence > g. opinion rule
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-264409-20260413:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. antonio sario y serrano and macario perez, jr. y mercado, accused; antonio sario y serrano, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. repealed. see instead comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640; see also am 18-03-16-sc) in illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs (secs. 5 and 11, ra 9165), the drug itself is the *corpus delicti*. the prosecution must prove its identity with moral certainty through an unbroken chain of custody covering the four links in *people v. kamad*: (1) seizure and marking by the apprehending officer; (2) turnover to the investigating officer; (3) turnover to the forensic chemist; and (4) turnover by the forensic chemist to the court. every person who handled the item must describe its condition and the precautions taken (*mallillin v. people*). reiterated.

**the third link is broken when the police officer who received the drugs at the crime laboratory is not presented**, leaving no evidence of the drugs' condition and safekeeping until the chemist retrieved them. **the fourth link is broken when the chemist's testimony is dispensed with by a stipulation covering only her qualifications, her receipt of the request and specimens, and the test results.** such a stipulation says nothing on how the drugs were handled, stored and preserved after examination and before submission to the court (*people v. supat*). these gaps create reasonable doubt and require acquittal. by contrast, the accused's failure to sign the inventory (when photographs show his presence) is inconsequential. so are markings that use only the accused's initials instead of the seizing officer's initials and the date, time and place required by the pnp manual, as long as they segregate the items from other evidence.

**under rule 122, section 11(a), a favorable judgment on appeal benefits a co-accused who did not appeal if it rests on a ground applicable to him. this holds even if he pleaded guilty to a lesser offense under a plea bargain and was convicted** (following *people v. cordova*). a broken chain of custody that renders all the drugs presented in the cases unreliable, including those underlying the co-accused's charges, is such a ground. viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 1. object or real evidence > c. chain of custody
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-258643-20260209:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. xxx258643, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > h. title viii – crimes against persons **refusing to heed the victim's expression of resistance constitutes force, whether the resistance is made prior to, at the beginning of, or in the middle of the sexual act.** sexual congress with a person who expressed resistance by words (telling the accused to stop) or deeds (trying to stand up while being held down) is rape under article 266-a of the rpc. resistance need not be tenacious: article 266-d accepts "[a]ny physical overt act manifesting resistance against the act of rape in any degree" as evidence, and the en banc rule in *people v. dulay* that tenacious resistance is not required was not overturned by *people v. tionloc* and *people v. cubay*. force need not be irresistible, and the age gap between an adult offender and a minor victim may place the offender in a position to force his will. "it is the job of this court to say what the law is; not how and when victims should resist sexual acts."

the **sweetheart theory** (reiterated) is an admission of carnal knowledge. the accused must prove by substantial evidence not only that he and the victim were lovers, but that she consented to the sexual act. a love affair does not justify rape.

applying *gramatica v. people* and *people v. xxx266039* (en banc, 2025), lascivious conduct against a minor aged 12 to below 18 falls under **section 5(b) of ra no. 7610 only if the child was "subjected to sexual abuse"**: the child indulged or engaged in the conduct (consented, though the consent is defective under the law), or was convinced, cajoled, or prevailed upon to take part because of the adult's "employment, use, persuasion, inducement, enticement or coercion." without such proof, the crime is **acts of lasciviousness under article 336 of the rpc**. because the resulting penalty was significantly lower than under ra no. 7610, the court awarded php 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages.
01-rosario-ponencias/am-mtj-26-056-20260:
anonymous, complainant, vs. judge elmer r. bernardo, municipal trial court in cities, batac city, ilocos norte, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 1. standards of ethical conduct of judges and justices > e. propriety (canon iv) judges must be beyond reproach in both their public and private lives. under **canon iv (propriety), sections 1 and 2 of the 2025 code of judicial conduct and accountability (cjca)**, a judge must freely and willingly accept personal restrictions that an ordinary citizen may find burdensome and must act consistently with the dignity of the judicial office. a judge must also refrain from any act, in or out of court, that may cause dishonor or ridicule to, or tend to tarnish, the judicial office. **a judge may be penalized even for conduct unrelated to official duties when it gravely tarnishes the public image of the judiciary.**

**a judge who, at around 2:30 a.m., threw a piece of wood and a stone that damaged his neighbors' parked vehicles, then defended himself with an implausible story (that he was aiming at a rat), is guilty of "prejudicial conduct that gravely besmirches or taints the reputation of the service," a serious offense under canon vii, section 18(k) of the cjca.** this offense reformulates "conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service": acts that tarnish the image and integrity of public office without a direct relation to official duties. even on the judge's own version, recklessly hurling objects where property could be damaged falls below the standard required of judges. an incredible defense, and "background facts" blaming the victims, show lack of remorse and worsen the judge's position.

the cjca applies to cases pending when it took effect (transitory clause). the quantum of proof is substantial evidence; technical rules do not strictly apply, but the respondent must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. under canon vii, section 22, a serious offense is punishable by dismissal, suspension, and/or a fine. where there is a mitigating circumstance such as first offense (sec. 24) and no aggravating circumstance, the court may impose a suspension or fine not less than half the minimum (sec. 25). the court imposed a fine of php 50,001.00. because a judge is also a lawyer, the court may separately remind him under canon ii, section 2 of the cpra (dignified conduct).
01-rosario-ponencias/am-rtj-19-2570-2026:
office of the court administrator, complainant, vs. winlove m. dumayas, former presiding judge, branch 59, regional trial court, makati city, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 2. accountability of members of the judiciary > a. judicial accountability and disciplinary proceedings (canon vii) **a judge is not administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law for an erroneous order issued in a judicial capacity, absent proof of bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or similar motive.** gross ignorance of the law is the disregard of basic rules and settled jurisprudence. where the law is straightforward and the facts evident, failing to know it or acting as if one does not know it is gross ignorance, without need to prove malice. otherwise, the order must not only be erroneous; it must be shown that the judge was moved by bad faith, dishonesty, hatred, or some like motive (reiterating cayabyab v. judge pangilinan, jr.). misreading a contractual provision that is not explicit, or issuing a wrong order that the judge later corrects on a motion for reconsideration, is an error of judgment, not gross ignorance. reversing oneself, by itself, is not an infraction, and ill motive cannot be presumed.

**the 2025 code of judicial conduct and accountability (cjca, a.m. no. 25-04-04-sc, effective december 21, 2025) applies to all pending and future cases** under its transitory clause (general provisions, section 1), unless the court finds that retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. **under section 23 of the cjca, a judge's separation from the service after the administrative case was instituted does not deprive the court of jurisdiction.** if the judge is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal, the court may impose, in lieu of dismissal, forfeiture of all or part of the benefits (never accrued leave credits) and disqualification from public office, and/or a fine.

settled rules restated in the analysis: once a compromise agreement is approved by a final order, it becomes a judgment that the court has the ministerial duty to enforce and cannot modify; and under article 2034 of the civil code, criminal liability cannot be the subject of a compromise. viii. obligations and contracts > b. contracts > 5. interpretation of contracts
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-276833-20260121:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. jose olbato y aurella, jaime toleva y camposano, romeo aruta y fabiano, rodrigo aruta y fabiano, alberto culanag y frejoles, spo4 romeo ayson y sejira @ "romy," po3 clayton patingan y amatic @ "ricky / bobot," edwin castillo y igada, lolita monarez y estrella, sebastian magaipo y alipante, mary-ann angcahan y butilla, jullien madrid y echavez @ "marlou," pepe bihag y baltazar, yong yong mentis (at large), vina argayoza (at large), and four john does, accused; jose olbato y aurella, jaime tolevas y camposano, romeo aruta y fabiano, rodrigo aruta y fabiano, and alberto culanag y frejoles, accused-appellants. iii. the revised penal code – book two > i. title ix – crimes against personal liberty and security the elements of **kidnapping for ransom under art. 267 of the revised penal code, as amended by ra 7659**, are: (1) the accused is a private person; (2) he or she kidnapped or detained, or in any manner deprived another of liberty; (3) the kidnapping or detention was illegal; and (4) the victim was kidnapped or detained for ransom. **a police officer who detains a person to extort ransom does not act in an official capacity**, so the first element is satisfied as to him (reiterating *people v. borja*).

**whether the ransom money was actually paid or received is of no moment, and the ransom money is not the corpus delicti** of kidnapping for ransom (reiterating *people v. jatulan*). its loss or non-presentation in court does not create reasonable doubt where the demand, negotiation and delivery are proved by testimonial and documentary evidence. conspiracy may be inferred from the concerted acts of the accused before, during and after the crime; a conspirator need not take part in every detail, as the act of one is the act of all.

denial and frame-up, like alibi, cannot prevail over positive identification; for alibi to prosper, the accused must prove that it was physically impossible for him to be at or near the crime scene, and an alibi corroborated only by acquaintances is viewed with suspicion (reiterated). **the death of an accused pending appeal extinguishes both his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto** (*people v. bayotas*), without prejudice to a separate civil action against his estate based on a source of obligation other than delict. vii. criminal procedure > c. prosecution of civil action (rule 111) > 4. civil liability ex delicto > b. when accused dies viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 4. positive and negative evidence
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-276927-20260119:
janito m. sedenio, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. iv. special penal laws > q. anti-violence against women and their children act (ra 9262, secs. 3–6 and 24–27) violence against women through harassment under **section 5(h)(5) of ra 9262** has three elements (reiterated, ang v. ca). (1) the offender has or had a sexual or dating relationship with the offended woman. (2) the offender, personally or through another, commits an act or series of acts of harassment against her. (3) the harassment causes her alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress. the first element is met **as long as, at the time of the crime, the offender and the woman were or used to be in a sexual or dating relationship.** a clandestine affair between two people married to others qualifies. the information need not allege that the relationship had already ended when the information was filed; that fact is immaterial.

**proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required. whether she suffered alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress is personal to her, so her testimony, if found credible, is sufficient to prove the third element** (applying araza v. people). no psychological report or expert testimony is needed.

text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them (rules on electronic evidence, rule 11, sec. 2). the recipient's testimony suffices. the accused's admission in open court that the sending number was his and that he sent the "humiliating [and] threatening" messages is a judicial admission. it binds him absent palpable mistake or proof that no such admission was made (rule 129, sec. 4). a rule 45 petition that lacks proof of service on the lower court or omits material dates may be dismissed on that ground alone (rule 45, secs. 3-5). viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 2. documentary evidence > e. electronic evidence (am 01-7-01-sc)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-269722-20260106:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. ronaldo infortuno, sr. y cruz, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > h. title viii – crimes against persons **reiterated:** the reliability of an out-of-court identification is tested by the **totality of circumstances**: (1) the witness's opportunity to view the criminal at the time of the crime; (2) the witness's degree of attention at that time; (3) the accuracy of any prior description given by the witness; (4) the length of time between the crime and the identification; (5) the level of certainty demonstrated by the witness at the identification; and (6) the suggestiveness of the identification procedure. the court also listed the twelve "danger signals" that tend to show an out-of-court identification may be erroneous (from *people v. jimenez*). **a photographic identification is not suggestive where the victim was shown photographs of different men every day, the accused was not singled out, and the victim immediately recognized him when she saw his photograph.** a two-month gap does not defeat the identification where the victim saw the assailant's face up close, including by the light of his flashlight, and was not distracted.

there is no standard reaction of a rape victim; failure to shout or call for help does not impair her credibility. "lust is no respecter of time or place": rape is not always committed in seclusion. the trial court's assessment of credibility is respected on appeal unless significant matters were overlooked, and it carries greater weight when affirmed by the ca (all reiterated).

rape under **article 266-a(1)(a) of the rpc**, as amended by ra 8353, requires (1) carnal knowledge of the victim, (2) accomplished through force, threat, or intimidation. a knife held to the victim's nape with a threat to hurt her if she screamed, followed by punches when she resisted, establishes force, threat, or intimidation. the penalty is reclusion perpetua (art. 266-b), with php 75,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, plus 6% annual interest from finality until full payment. viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 3. competent and credible evidence xii. damages > c. other kinds of damages
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-255485-20251126:
ian solis y aquino, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. ii. the revised penal code – book one > a. felonies > 4. stages of execution > c. attempted, frustrated, and consummated stages **whether an injury is fatal is a question of fact. absent testimony from the attending physician that the injury would have caused the victim's death without timely medical assistance, the court cannot presume that it is fatal, even if the medico-legal certificate shows that vital organs were involved or that significant blood loss occurred, "since what may be fatal for one person may not be fatal for another."** in a prosecution for frustrated homicide, the victim's wounds must be proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the physician who attended to them. a medical certificate is merely the opinion of one who must first be established as an expert, and the defense must be able to cross-examine its author; a stipulation on the certificate's existence is not enough. the doubt on the character of the wounds is resolved in favor of the accused, so the crime is only **attempted homicide** (reiterating *etino v. people* and *oliveros v. people*).

circumstantial evidence suffices to convict under **rule 133, section 4** when (a) there is more than one circumstance, (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. the circumstances must form an unbroken chain pointing to the accused, to the exclusion of all others, as the guilty person (reiterated).

voluntary surrender is not appreciated when the accused gives himself up only after the police come to his house, tell his family he is a suspect, and ask his parents to surrender him; the surrender must be spontaneous. treachery proven at trial but not alleged in the information cannot qualify the crime to murder, but it supports an award of exemplary damages; the court reiterated *people v. solar*'s reminder to prosecutors to allege attendant circumstances with particularity. viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 2. direct and circumstantial evidence ii. the revised penal code – book one > b. criminal liability > 8. circumstances affecting criminal liability > c. mitigating circumstances vii. criminal procedure > b. prosecution of offenses (rule 110) > 6. complaint or information > b. sufficiency > ii. designation of the offense; qualifying and aggravating circumstances
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-260860-20251111:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. xxx (g.r. no. 260860), accused-appellant. vii. criminal procedure > n. appeal (rule 122) **when the accused appeals a conviction for a lesser offense, he waives the constitutional safeguard against double jeopardy both as to that conviction and as to the implied acquittal of the original (greater) charge. the whole case is thrown open to review, and the appellate court may convict him of the original charge** (here, statutory rape instead of acts of lasciviousness). the court reiterated the "absolute waiver" theory consistently applied in philippine jurisprudence (trono v. united states; ko bu lin v. ca; people v. carreon; people v. rondero, all citing lontoc v. people), which is reflected in rule 124, section 11 (the ca may "increase or reduce the penalty"). the rule that a "downgraded" conviction can no longer be reviewed applies only when the **state** appeals (kepner; people v. dela torre) or, as in people v. alarcon, in an automatic review in which the accused had no hand. the court clarified that people v. arcega (a state appeal) erred in relying on people v. balunsat (an accused's appeal), and noted that the balunsat doctrine had already been abandoned (people v. xxx262846, g.r. no. 262846, february 18, 2025, en banc).

an information alleging that rape was committed "on or about the year 2015" is defective: under people v. ladrillo it covers the year and the years immediately before and after, so the accused must account for up to 36 months. the remedy is a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash because the information does not conform substantially to the prescribed form (rule 117, sec. 3(e)). the court clarified that **a defective information is not "cured" by evidence at trial. it is quashed, amended, or waived.** this ground is not among the non-waivable grounds in rule 117, section 9, so it is waived if not raised before arraignment and cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

on consummation, the court reiterated people v. agao (en banc, 2022). "mere touching" means the penis penetrating the cleft of the labia majora, however slightly. with pre-pubescent victims, an attempt to penetrate likely indicates at least introduction into the vulval cleft. where a child does not explicitly describe penetration, courts may find consummation from attendant circumstances, such as the victim's testimony that she felt pain in her genitals. viii. constitutional rights > s. right against double jeopardy iii. the revised penal code – book two > h. title viii – crimes against persons
01-rosario-ponencias/am-rtj-26-119-20251:
atty. pablo b. francisco, complainant, vs. hon. miguel s. asuncion, presiding judge, branch 99, regional trial court, antipolo city, rizal, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 2. accountability of members of the judiciary > a. judicial accountability and disciplinary proceedings (canon vii) **undue delay in rendering a decision is a form of negligence that may be gross neglect of duty (a serious charge) or simple neglect of duty (a less serious charge) under rule 140 of the rules of court, as amended by a.m. no. 21-08-09-sc.** lower courts must decide cases within three months from submission (article viii, section 15(1), 1987 constitution), and judges must deliver reserved decisions efficiently, fairly and with reasonable promptness (canon 6, section 5, new code of judicial conduct). **a judge who cannot meet the period must ask the court, through the oca, for an extension** (oca circular no. 243-2022). heavy caseload, the pandemic, duties as executive or assisting judge, and family health concerns do not excuse the delay when the judge never sought an extension and decided long after regular court operations resumed. deciding the case later does not erase liability, and the judge cannot avoid the charge by saying the complainant should have appealed: the issue is the delay, not the merits (reiterated).

simple neglect of duty is punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than php 35,000 but not exceeding php 100,000 (rule 140, section 15(b), in relation to section 17(2)). a previous administrative liability for which a penalty was imposed is an aggravating circumstance (section 19), allowing a penalty of up to double the maximum (section 20). the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence. the judge is not separately liable as a member of the bar for the same delay without evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. vi. judicial department > e. the supreme court > 1. composition, powers, and functions > b. administrative supervision over lower courts
01-rosario-ponencias/am-23-08-55-rtc-202:
re: dropping from the rolls of ms. mailyn e. miras, stenographer iii, branch 65, regional trial court, infanta, quezon. xi. law on public officers > b. public office > 9. termination of official relation under **rule 20, section 132(a-1) of the 2025 rules on administrative cases in the civil service (raccs)** (csc resolution no. 2500357), **an official or employee who is continuously absent without official leave (awol) for at least 30 working days may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice.** a notice of separation is issued at the employee's last known address, and the employee may appeal within 15 days from receipt. failure to provide the notice does not invalidate the dropping, but the appeal period then runs from actual receipt of the notice.

**dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary** (2025 raccs, rule 20, section 135): it does not forfeit any benefit or disqualify the employee from reemployment in the government. its purpose is to address the disruption caused by continuous and prolonged awol by declaring the post vacant so it can be filled. hence, the dismissal of criminal cases against the employee is irrelevant.

**approval of a vacation leave is not presumed**; it depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of office, so the mere filing of a leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent. medical or psychological problems, or a feeling of being bullied by a supervisor, do not excuse an employee who stops reporting without waiting for the leave to be approved. the court applied these settled rules and denied the appeal with finality.
01-rosario-ponencias/oca-ipi-20-3112-mtj:
editha m. bayona, complainant, vs. hon. aida theresita b. basa-diviva, presiding judge, municipal circuit trial court, sta. cruz-candelaria, zambales, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 2. accountability of members of the judiciary > a. judicial accountability and disciplinary proceedings (canon vii) **as a matter of policy, the acts of a judge in a judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action, however erroneous, as long as the judge acted in good faith. only judicial errors tainted with fraud, dishonesty, gross ignorance, bad faith, or deliberate intent to do injustice are administratively sanctioned** (reiterating pitney v. judge abrogar). errors committed in the exercise of adjudicative functions must be corrected through judicial remedies, not administrative proceedings. disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement, or substitute for judicial remedies, and an inquiry into administrative liability arising from judicial acts may be made only after the other available remedies have been settled. bias and partiality require a showing of arbitrariness or prejudice.

**in administrative cases, the complainant bears the burden of proving the charges by substantial evidence.** bare allegations cannot overcome the presumption that the judge regularly performed official duties. requiring proof protects magistrates from flimsy and unsubstantiated charges.

procedural rules reiterated and applied: (a) issuing a hold-departure order is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the rtc (oca circular no. 39-97), so a first-level judge who issued one "would have reeked of ignorance of the law" (re: occiano); (b) under a.m. no. 05-8-26-sc, first-level court judges no longer conduct preliminary investigations, which are now with the provincial or city prosecutor, and unjust vexation, a light offense, does not require one; (c) the private complainant need not be present at the arraignment unless the court requires it (rule 116, sec. 1(f)). a judge whose postponements were not shown to be whimsical, but who was not cautious enough in granting them, may be admonished. viii. constitutional rights > g. liberty of abode and right to travel > 2. watchlist, hold departure orders, and precautionary hold departure orders
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-255749-20251015:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. jeryl bautista y martinez, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. repealed. see instead comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640) in illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs, the drug itself is the corpus delicti. the first link in the chain of custody requires compliance with section 21 of ra 9165, as amended by ra 10640, under the **nisperos guidelines (reiterated)**. marking must be done immediately upon confiscation, at the place of confiscation, and in the presence of the offender. inventory and photography must be done immediately after seizure, in the presence of the accused and, for seizures from august 7, 2014, an elected public official and a representative of the national prosecution service or the media. "immediately" carries a **time requirement** (no unreasonable delay or intervening period) and a **place requirement** (at the place of arrest). any deviation must be acknowledged and justified by the prosecution, which must also show that the integrity of the items was preserved.

**where the officers made the accused wait 10 to 15 minutes for the insulating witnesses to arrive before marking, inventorying and photographing the sachet sold, the marking was not "immediate." the witnesses' absence at the time of seizure is not a justifiable ground, because they should have been present or near the place of seizure from the start** (people v. ramos). the seizure and custody of that item are void, its integrity is compromised, and the accused must be acquitted of illegal sale.

**the plain view doctrine only supplements an existing justification for a warrantless search** (people v. musa). compliance with it is not always required, especially when the search is limited to the person of the accused, where items are usually hidden. drugs found in a frisk incident to a lawful arrest in flagrante delicto are admissible if the ridon requisites are met: (a) a lawful arrest; (b) a warrantless search made after it; (c) limited to the person of the accused and the area within his immediate control; and (d) done at the place of arrest. vii. criminal procedure > o. search and seizure (rule 126) > 2. warrantless search > b. plain view doctrine viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 1. object or real evidence > c. chain of custody viii. constitutional rights > c. right against unreasonable searches and seizures > 2. warrantless arrests and searches

roxaco-asia hospitality corporation [formerly roxaco-vanguard hotel corp.], petitioner, vs. gulf canary construction and development, inc. and asia united insurance, inc., respondents. iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > d. issues cognizable under **section 19 of executive order no. 1008** (construction industry arbitration law), a ciac arbitral award is **final and unappealable except on questions of law**. reiterating *global medical center of laguna, inc. v. ross systems international, inc.*, the court held that the ciac's factual findings may be reviewed only on narrow, **"tribunal-centered" and not "fact-centered"** grounds: (1) a challenge to the integrity of the arbitral tribunal, i.e., (i) the award was procured by corruption, fraud or other undue means; (ii) evident partiality or corruption of the arbitrators; (iii) misconduct in refusing to postpone the hearing upon sufficient cause or in refusing to hear pertinent and material evidence; (iv) an arbitrator disqualified under section 9 of ra 876 wilfully refrained from disclosing it, or other misbehavior materially prejudiced a party; or (v) the arbitrators exceeded their powers or so imperfectly executed them that no mutual, final and definite award was made; and (2) an allegation that the tribunal violated the constitution or positive law. **mere disagreement with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence, or perceived errors of fact, does not open the award to review.** a party invoking partiality or ground (v) must satisfactorily show that the arbitrators were compromised or that their integrity could not be relied upon.

the reviewing court asks two questions. first, is the issue one of law or of fact? if of law, the award may be appealed. second, if of fact, is it only a disagreement with the tribunal's factual conclusions (not reviewable), or does it go into the integrity of the tribunal in a manner amounting to grave abuse of discretion (reviewable)? **whether undisputed and authentic documents legally amount to an agreement to extend the completion date, or to a waiver of the contractual notice requirement for an extension, is a question of law.** who caused the delay, whether the grounds for termination existed, and how much of the downpayment or rectification cost remains due are questions of fact. (the court noted that *global medical center*'s ruling on the modes of review, rule 45 to the supreme court on questions of law and rule 65 to the ca on factual issues involving grave abuse, applies prospectively and did not govern this case, but its exposition of reviewable factual issues applies squarely.)

on the merits: a **waiver must be clear and unequivocal**, and there is no implied waiver without a clear, unequivocal and decisive act. letting the contractor continue working past the completion date, agreeing to acceleration measures, and extending the performance bond do not waive the contract's extension-of-time procedure, because a contractor's delay does not end the contract; it only makes the contractor liable for delay damages while its duty to finish remains, and an owner who keeps the project going is mitigating damages under **article 2203 of the civil code**. attorney's fees under **article 2208** and costs of arbitration cannot be awarded without a finding that the losing party resisted the claim in bad faith (reiterated). viii. obligations and contracts > a. obligations > 2. nature and effects of obligations > a. breaches of obligations; remedies xii. damages > b. actual and compensatory damages > 4. attorney’s fees and expenses of litigation ix. special contracts > d. credit transactions > 3. guaranty and suretyship > c. extinguishment
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-259037-20250929:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. maricris bazar y bello, accused-appellant. viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 2. direct and circumstantial evidence **circumstantial evidence suffices to convict only if (a) there is more than one circumstance; (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven; and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt** (rule 133, rules of court; reiterating people v. modesto). the circumstances must form an unbroken chain leading to one fair and reasonable conclusion that points to the accused, to the exclusion of all others. **when the inculpatory facts can be explained in two or more ways, one of which is consistent with innocence, the evidence fails the test of moral certainty and cannot support a conviction.** under people v. monje, circumstantial evidence must be acted on with caution; all essential facts must be consistent with guilt; the facts must exclude every other theory; and they must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. because circumstantial evidence is only as strong as its weakest link, the prosecution must rely on the strength of its own case, not on the weakness of the defense.

**flight per se does not establish guilt; it only tends to do so.** it must be coupled with other direct or circumstantial evidence, because it is inherently ambiguous and may have innocent explanations (fear of retribution, unwillingness to testify, fear of being wrongly apprehended). flight that came only after the accused learned of a pursuit and a reward for her capture, after she had stayed beside the crime scene for hours, does not show a guilty conscience.

a blood-stained weapon and clothes found in a house occupied by about ten other people do not link the accused to the crime when no evidence traces the blood to the victims and nothing shows she wielded the weapon. dna results that were not formally offered (and not recited in a stipulated testimony) cannot be considered. the court observed that in a case resting purely on circumstantial evidence, the trial court could have ordered dna testing **motu proprio** under section 4 of the rule on dna evidence, even if samples had already been tested at the police's request. viii. constitutional rights > m. rights of the accused
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-215129-20250929:
lapuy battalion employees agrarian reform beneficiaries cooperative (labearbco), represented by its chairman, marcos endrina, petitioner, vs. enrica o. babao, julius antonius babao co, maria rosalie babao co, maria conception babao co, josephine babao co, maria elena babao co, anthony cris co, enrico tajanlangit, ana rica c. cacho, mar vince emmanuel c. reyes, and john lee vincent c. reyes, respondents. iii. civil procedure > t. execution, satisfaction, and effect of judgments (rule 39) > 7. effect of judgments or final orders **a person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a case to which he was not made a party. a writ of execution may be issued only against a party, not against one who did not have his day in court** (*green acres holdings v. cabral*). this principle conforms to the constitutional guarantee of due process. an adjudicator gravely abuses its discretion when it consolidates a new case against holders of derivative titles with an old, final case and orders the old judgment implemented against them, instead of deciding the new case on the merits. doing so treats the new case as a mere motion for execution and binds the titleholders without a hearing.

**a torrens title cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding (sec. 48, pd 1529).** an attack is direct when the object of the action is to annul or set aside the title, and collateral when it is made as an incident in an action for a different relief (*hortizuela v. tagufa*). cancelling the derivative titles of persons who were not impleaded, by implementing a judgment that only annulled an extrajudicial settlement of estate, is a prohibited collateral attack. the court agreed with the ca that the agrarian adjudicator (rarad) had no jurisdiction to entertain the action for cancellation of certificates of title issued to third persons. reiterated. vi. land titles and deeds (pd 1529, as amended by ra 6732 and 11573) > f. certificate of title viii. constitutional rights > a. due process > 2. judicial and administrative due process
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-257105-20250827:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. rudy peralta y mabbonag, cesar liban y peralta, philip soriano y pasion, adviento soriano y pasion, roberto soriano y pasion, ferdinand soriano y pasion alias 'mar,' and napoleon liban (at large), accused; rudy peralta y mabbonag and cesar liban y peralta, accused-appellants. vii. criminal procedure > b. prosecution of offenses (rule 110) > 6. complaint or information > d. amendment and substitution **before the accused pleads, an information may be amended in form or in substance without leave of court, and the amended information ipso facto supersedes the original. no motion to admit it and no order admitting it are needed** (rule 110, section 14, rules of court). the exception is an amendment before plea that downgrades the nature of the offense or excludes an accused. that kind of amendment may be made only on the prosecutor's motion, with notice to the offended party and with leave of court. the court likened the rule to a plaintiff's right to amend a complaint before a responsive pleading is served, where the amended pleading supersedes the original without an order of admission (rule 10, section 8). a later court order "admitting" such an amended information is "a superfluity."

**changing an information from frustrated murder to murder after the victim dies is only a formal amendment.** frustrated murder is a stage in the execution of murder and is necessarily included in it. the victim's death is a supervening fact that bears only on the penalty, and every defense available under the original information remains available (reiterating *teehankee, jr. v. madayag*). such an amendment needs no new preliminary investigation and **no re-arraignment**. the purpose of arraignment, to inform the accused of the nature and cause of the accusation, was already served at the first arraignment.

when an accused-appellant dies before final judgment, his criminal liability and his civil liability ex delicto are totally extinguished (article 89(1), revised penal code; *people v. bayotas*). claims for civil liability based on other sources of obligation are not affected. ii. the revised penal code – book one > d. extinction of criminal liability > 1. total extinction > a. death of convict
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-263615-20250819:
petronilo solomon sarigumba, petitioner, vs. commission on elections, represented by campaign finance unit, respondent. viii. constitutional rights > n. rights to speedy trial and speedy disposition of cases the right to a speedy disposition of cases under **article iii, section 16 of the constitution** may be invoked in a preliminary investigation conducted by the comelec. applying *cagang v. sandiganbayan*, once the delay goes beyond the prescribed periods, **the burden shifts to the prosecution** to prove that it followed the prescribed procedure, that the complexity of the issues and the volume of evidence made the delay inevitable, and that the respondent suffered no prejudice.

**a respondent's failure to file a counter-affidavit does not give the comelec license to delay the preliminary investigation indefinitely.** rule 34, sections 6 and 8 of the comelec rules of procedure must be read together: if the respondent does not file a counter-affidavit within the 10-day period, the investigating officer must resolve the complaint on the complainant's evidence, and **the 20-day period to conclude the preliminary investigation (plus five days to resolve) is counted from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit**. a delay of over six years in resolving a simple overspending complaint against one respondent, decided only on his own statement of election contributions and expenditures (soce), is inordinate. the court applied *peñas v. comelec* and *peralta v. comelec* even though the respondents there filed counter-affidavits and the petitioner here did not.

reiterating *peñas* and *cervantes v. sandiganbayan*, a respondent is not duty-bound to follow up his case, and he may invoke the right after the adverse resolution, unless the delay is directly attributable to him. because inordinate delay alone merits dismissal, a prior motion for reconsideration may be dispensed with. the remedy is the **nullification of the resolution finding probable cause and the dismissal of the complaint**. xii. election law > g. power to prosecute election offenses (bp 881, sec. 265, as amended by ra 9369; exclude penal provisions) v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-260664-20250818:
development bank of the philippines, represented by its general santos city branch head, mariela luz t. cortez, petitioner, vs. manuel te, respondent. iii. civil procedure > t. execution, satisfaction, and effect of judgments (rule 39) > 1. immutability of final judgments; exceptions **a judgment finding a person guilty of indirect contempt, once final and executory, is immutable. the trial court cannot later lift it, or remove the penalties it imposed, because the contemnor has since (even partly) complied with the order he disobeyed.** under the doctrine of finality or immutability of judgments, a final decision may no longer be modified in any respect, even to correct erroneous conclusions of fact or law. any amendment that substantially affects it is null and void for lack of jurisdiction, as are the proceedings held for that purpose (industrial management international development corp. v. nlrc; eusebio v. csc, reiterated). an order that is worded as a recognition of compliance but in practice nullifies the final contempt judgment is an impermissible modification, and an appellate court that affirms it commits grave abuse of discretion.

contempt is direct (committed in the presence of or so near the judge as to obstruct the administration of justice) or indirect (willful disobedience of the lawful process or order of the court). contempt proceedings are sui generis. they are civil when the dominant purpose is remedial, to compel obedience to an order for the benefit of a party, and criminal when it is punitive, to vindicate the dignity and authority of the court (lorenzo shipping, reiterated). **even when the contempt is civil in nature, the final judgment imposing it can no longer be disturbed.**
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-257251-20250818:
banco maximo, inc., petitioner, vs. chris angelo c. pelayo, mary ann c. pelayo-calisura, and catherine c. pelayo-soco, respondents. iii. family relations > b. family relations > 5. family home a family home is the dwelling house where the spouses, or an unmarried head of a family, and their family reside, together with the land on which it stands. it is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and it is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (articles 152 and 153, family code). **but the exemption is not automatic: it must be timely and properly asserted by the proper party.** the claim must be set up and proved to the sheriff before the public auction (*honrado v. court of appeals*; *taruc v. maximo*), or at the latest within a reasonable time, that is, before the one-year redemption period expires (*spouses fortaleza v. spouses lapitan*). failure to do so estops the claimant. the court reiterated these rules.

**the right to claim the exemption is a personal privilege.** heirs who, through a voluntary extrajudicial settlement, waived all their interest in the property in favor of a co-heir before he mortgaged it have no standing to invoke the family home exemption to annul the mortgage and foreclosure. this is especially so when they raise it only after the auction and after failed attempts to redeem. a mortgagee bank that lent in good faith, relying on a tax declaration in the mortgagor's name and without notice of any adverse claim, is protected.

in any event, **under article 155(3) of the family code, a family home is not exempt from execution for debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether constituted before or after the family home.** a property's character as a family home does not by itself invalidate a mortgage or a foreclosure conducted in accordance with law. on procedure: when a court annuls a deed (here, the extrajudicial settlement) whose nullity no party alleged or prayed for, its judgment goes beyond the pleadings and is "extrajudicial and void." iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > e. modes > v. appeal by certiorari to sc (rule 45)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-264132-20250813:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. yyy, zzz (acquitted), and xxx, accused; xxx, accused-appellant. iv. special penal laws > p. anti-trafficking in persons act (ra 9208, secs. 3–6 and 10–12, as amended by ra 10364, 11862, and 12312) trafficking in persons under **section 4(a) of ra no. 9208, as amended by ra no. 10364**, has three elements (reiterating *people v. casio*): (1) the **act**: recruitment, obtaining, hiring, providing, offering, transportation, transfer, maintaining, harboring, or receipt of persons, "with or without the victim's consent or knowledge"; (2) the **means**: threat, force or other coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power or position, taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person, or giving or receiving payments or benefits to achieve the consent of one having control over another; and (3) the **purpose**: exploitation or prostitution of others, other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labor, slavery, servitude, or removal or sale of organs. the crime is **qualified under section 6(a)** when the trafficked person is a child.

**the law punishes the mere receipt of persons for the purpose of trafficking, regardless of the victim's consent or knowledge.** a bar manager who hired and supervised a minor is liable even if she is not the owner of the bar and even if others brought the minor to her. acts of trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of the establishment, and registered ownership by itself does not create criminal liability (*people v. villanueva*). the means element is met by **taking advantage of the victim's vulnerability as a minor** (*people v. de dios*), so the minor's admission that she was not forced to work and could have refused does not defeat the charge. allowing customers to take the minor out for sex and collecting the "bar fine" establishes the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation.
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-262644-20250813:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. james williams y francis and joy montecillo y butaslac, accused, joy montecillo y butaslac, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. repealed. see instead comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640; see also am 18-03-16-sc) in illegal sale of dangerous drugs (sec. 5, ra 9165), the drug is the corpus delicti. the prosecution must account for every link in the chain of custody from seizure to presentation in court (reiterated). **for seizures before august 7, 2014 (before ra 10640), section 21 of ra 9165 requires the inventory and photographing to be done immediately after seizure in the presence of the accused and three insulating witnesses: an elected public official, a doj representative, and a media representative.** under the nisperos v. people guidelines, any deviation must be positively acknowledged by the prosecution. the prosecution must then prove (1) justifiable grounds for non-compliance and (2) the preservation of the integrity and evidentiary value of the seized items.

**a growing crowd, a thickly populated place of arrest, or approaching darkness is not a justifiable ground** for skipping the inventory at the place of arrest when no actual threat to the team's safety is substantiated. this is especially so where the team was large and heavily armed (here, 15 agents). failing to make earnest efforts to secure the witnesses, despite hours of waiting before the arrest, and **leaving out the doj representative with no explanation other than the team leader's instruction**, are unjustified deviations. they compromise the integrity of the seized drug and warrant acquittal, so the court need not examine the other links.

the death of an accused before his conviction becomes final requires dismissal of the criminal case against him. viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 1. object or real evidence > c. chain of custody
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-256964-20250813:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. ariston paterno, jr. y sales, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. repealed. see instead comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640; see also am 18-03-16-sc) **while the imposable penalty for illegal possession of five grams or more but less than 10 grams of shabu under section 11(2) of ra 9165 is 20 years and one day to life imprisonment, the maximum of life imprisonment may be imposed only when the circumstances in section 13 are present**, i.e., the accused was found "possessing any dangerous drug during a party, or at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least [two] persons." otherwise, a maximum term **below** life imprisonment must be imposed so the accused can avail of the indeterminate sentence law, which by its section 2 does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. the court followed *people v. pis-an* and the reasoning in then justice peralta's concurring opinion in *people v. obias*, which it quoted, and imposed 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum, where there was neither allegation nor proof of a section 13 circumstance.

on chain of custody (reiterated): for offenses committed while ra 10640 was in effect, the inventory need only be witnessed by the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the national prosecution service **or** the media; a doj representative is not required. following *people v. casa*, marking, inventory and photographing must be done at the place of seizure unless the safety of the officers, the witnesses or the items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger. **that the accused became unruly and his sister and friends caused a commotion is not a justifiable ground to do the marking and inventory at the police station**; the unjustified deviation renders the seizure and custody void, compromises the integrity of the drugs, and warrants acquittal. drugs found in a later search at the police station, immediately marked and inventoried there before the required witnesses, and traced through an unbroken chain of custody, may still support a conviction for possession. ii. the revised penal code – book one > c. penalties > 5. determination of imposable penalty > a. indeterminate sentence law (act 4103, as amended) viii. evidence > e. kinds (rule 130) > 1. object or real evidence > c. chain of custody
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-249916-20250813:
national bureau of investigation, region vii, petitioner, vs. avelino j. gungob, sr., respondent. xi. law on public officers > d. accountability of public officers (ra 6713) > 2. discipline > a. grounds **misconduct is a transgression of an established and definite rule of action, more particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer. it is grave only if it involves corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or disregard of established rules, proved by substantial evidence; otherwise it is simple** (*csc v. ledesma*). a person charged with grave misconduct may be held liable for simple misconduct. plain unlawful behavior by a public officer, even without bad faith, malice or corrupt motive, already constitutes simple misconduct, because **good faith is not a defense to simple misconduct** (*faeldonea v. csc*). a mayor who directed the extraction and hauling of limestone without the required permits, a prima facie violation of section 103 of the philippine mining act (ra 7942), is liable for simple misconduct. it does not matter that the materials were used for bona fide municipal projects or that he had repeatedly asked the province to renew the municipality's gratuitous permit.

**when a party is represented by counsel, judgments and other papers must be served on counsel (rule 13, sec. 2, 1997 and 2019 rules). notice to the party itself is not notice in law and does not start the reglementary period.** a government agency represented by the osg has 15 days from the osg's receipt of the decision, not from the agency's own earlier receipt, to move for reconsideration. reiterated (*soriano v. soriano*; *villalongha v. ca*). iii. civil procedure > e. pleadings > 10. filing and service (rules 13 and 13-a, as amended; am 10-3-7-sc, 11-9-4-sc, 25-01-13-sc, and 25-09-16-sc)
01-rosario-ponencias/ac-13998-20250813:
marife c. manongsong, complainant, vs. atty. ariel m. reyes, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > a. legal ethics (cpra) > 9. discipline and disbarment of lawyers (canon vi) > c. charges and sanctions **a lawyer who issues a check that is later dishonored for having been drawn against a closed account, and who reneges on repeated promises to pay a just debt, commits gross misconduct** in violation of canon ii, sections 1 (proper conduct) and 2 (dignified conduct) of the code of professional responsibility and accountability (cpra). such conduct shows "a lack of personal honesty and good moral character as to render him or her unworthy of public confidence" (reiterating *wilkie v. atty. limos*, *lao v. atty. medel* and *tan v. atty. pangan*). gross misconduct is a serious offense punishable by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding php 100,000.00, or a combination (canon vi, section 33 in relation to section 37).

the court may temper the penalty by appreciating mitigating circumstances under canon vi, section 38(a), including expression of remorse, humanitarian considerations and other analogous circumstances. **the lawyer's plea acknowledging a "wrong personal economic decision aggravated by the pandemic," the adverse impact of the covid-19 pandemic on lawyers in private practice, and his partial payment (the first php 500,000.00 check cleared) justified a suspension of only six months**, consistent with *egger v. atty. duran*, which reduced a one-year suspension to six months because of financial hardship caused by typhoon yolanda.

**a lawyer's unjustified failure to obey the ibp's orders in the disciplinary case** (to file a mandatory conference brief, appear at the mandatory conference, and file a position paper) **violates canon iii, section 2 and is a less serious offense under canon vi, section 34(c)**, punishable by suspension of one to six months, a fine of php 35,000.00 to php 100,000.00, or both. it is **a separate and distinct offense**, unrelated to the mitigating circumstances appreciated on the main charge; following *grand pillar international development, inc. v. atty. cruz*, the court imposed a php 50,000.00 fine. these are reiterated rules applied under the cpra.
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-220087-20250811:
hacienda san isidro / silos farms and rey silos llamado, petitioners, vs. lucito villaruel and helen villaruel, respondents. iii. employment relationship > a. employer-employee relationship > 2. determination of employer-employee relationship > a. fourfold test on the employer's motion for reconsideration, the court **maintained** the two requisites for regular seasonal employment laid down in its november 13, 2023 decision: (1) seasonal work or services; and (2) employment for more than one season. it also kept the rule that pakyaw pay does not negate regular employment if the employer has the right to control. it nonetheless **set aside the decision and reversed the ca**, because the worker never proved that right.

**under the control test, the employer must reserve the right to control not only the end achieved but also the manner and means used to reach it. the worker claiming benefits bears the burden of proving that right by substantial evidence, and the control must be of a level that interferes with the means and methods of accomplishing the assigned tasks.** rules that merely serve as guidelines toward a mutually desired result, without dictating means and methods, do not establish an employment relationship. the fact that a person works on the alleged employer's farm does not automatically mean the farm owner controlled, or reserved the right to control, the means and methods of the work. the court clarified *gapayao v. fulo* on two points:
- *gapayao* applied the control test incompletely. it presumed control from farm ownership and the right to review the quality of output, which shows control of the end only.
- *gapayao* misappreciated *mercado*. freedom to offer services to other farm owners was merely an added observation of the labor arbiter in *mercado*, not its ratio decidendi. *mercado* rested on on-and-off hiring.

**art. 295 (formerly art. 280) of the labor code is not a criterion for determining whether an employer-employee relationship exists.** it only distinguishes regular from casual employees, and it does not apply where the relationship itself is disputed. the following do not by themselves prove employment: length of service, repeated assignment of tasks, and receipt of wages, which is only one prong of the four-fold test. in a rule 45 petition, uniform factual findings of the la, nlrc and ca bind the court only if supported by substantial evidence. factual review is allowed in exceptional cases. iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > e. modes > v. appeal by certiorari to sc (rule 45)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-267815-20250806:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. zzz, accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > h. title viii – crimes against persons > 1. all except arts. 260–261 **statutory rape** under article 266-a(1)(d) of the revised penal code, as amended by ra 8353, requires only that (1) the offended party is under 12 years of age and (2) the accused had carnal knowledge of her, whether or not there was force, threat, intimidation or grave abuse of authority. consent is immaterial; the only questions are the victim's age and whether carnal knowledge took place (reiterated). a rape victim's straightforward testimony that conforms with the medico-legal findings is enough to prove penetration. minor inconsistencies between witnesses do not destroy their credibility, and denial cannot prevail over positive identification.

ra 11648 (2022) raised the age for statutory rape to under 16. it added a close-in-age exemption (an age difference of not more than three years, with a sexual act proven consensual, non-abusive and non-exploitative), which does not apply if the victim is under 13, and it did not amend article 266-b. **because ra 11648 is not favorable to the accused, it does not retroact (art. 22, rpc). a rape committed before it took effect is judged under article 266-a as amended by ra 8353 alone.**

statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua. under a.m. no. 15-08-02-sc, the phrase "without eligibility for parole" is used only when the death penalty would have been imposed but for ra 9346; otherwise it must be deleted. under people v. jugueta, where the penalty is reclusion perpetua (and not death reduced by ra 9346), civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages are php 75,000.00 each, with 6% interest per annum from finality. viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 4. positive and negative evidence
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-255113-20250806:
heirs of benita yanzon cipriano, represented by ma. dorothy arlene cipriano, petitioners, vs. national transmission corporation (transco), respondent. v. special civil actions > g. expropriation (rule 67; ra 10752, as amended by ra 12289) > 3. just compensation **just compensation is determined as of the date of the taking of the property or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first (rule 67, section 4).** this general rule applies even in inverse condemnation, where the government entered without filing expropriation proceedings. *npc v. heirs of macabangkit sangkay* and *npc v. saludares* reckoned value from the owner's filing of the inverse condemnation suit. those rulings are exceptions justified only by special circumstances: stealth (underground tunnels the owners did not know of), or the expropriator's refusal to acknowledge the claim because it insisted it had already paid. they do not apply to **visible high-tension transmission lines**, whose existence the owners cannot claim to be unaware of. this is especially so where the expropriator invokes a right of way granted by the owner's predecessor. reiterated (*ntc v. oroville*; *ntc v. religious of the virgin mary*).

the value at the time of taking must be computed with the **present value formula** of *republic v. spouses nocom* and *heirs of jose mariano v. city of naga* (en banc), which accounts for the owner's opportunity loss from non-payment. the total just compensation then earns 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment. **consequential damages to the remaining portions are a component of just compensation.** they are likewise reckoned from the taking under the same formula.

01-rosario-ponencias/gr-241587-20250806:

carolina bautista-pangilinan, represented by miriam b. bustamante, complainant, vs. atty. engracio m. icasiano, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > a. legal ethics (cpra) > 8. duties and responsibilities of lawyers (cpra) > c. propriety (canon ii) **forum shopping** is the repetitive availment of several judicial remedies in different courts, simultaneously or successively, all substantially founded on the same transactions and the same essential facts and circumstances, and all raising substantially the same issues either pending in or already resolved adversely by some other court. the ultimate test is the vexation caused to the courts and the parties by asking different fora to rule on the same or related causes or to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, creating the possibility of conflicting decisions (reiterated).

01-rosario-ponencias/am-rtj-25-099-20250:
corpus b. alzate, complainant, vs. hon. raphiel f. alzate, presiding judge, branch 1, regional trial court, bangued, abra, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 1. standards of ethical conduct of judges and justices > d. impartiality (canon iii) > i. mandatory vs. voluntary inhibition (see also rule 137) **a judge must inhibit from a case in which his spouse acted as counsel. under rule 137, section 1 of the rules of court and canon iii, section 5 and canon iv, section 4 of the new code of judicial conduct, the inhibition is "not merely discretionary; it is compulsory."** canon iv, section 4 provides that judges "shall not participate in the determination of a case in which any member of their family represents a litigant or is associated in any manner with the case." **the spouse's withdrawal as counsel when the judge took over the case does not cure the disqualification.** she had actively participated before withdrawing (she prepared and filed the petition and presented the petitioner's evidence-in-chief), so a perception that the case was decided in her favor remains. a judge should not handle a case where there is a perception, rightly or wrongly, that he is susceptible to bias because of relationship.

people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. herminio casal reyes, municipal mayor, ma. marley c. daday, leo bausing gomez, arturo elumba estil, joel dingle plaza, romeo o. magadan (all) member, sangguniang bayan, virgilio a. julao, member, sangguniang bayan/acting presiding officer, filomeno caseñas salise, municipal treasurer, (all of) loreto, agusan del sur, accused; herminio casal reyes, ma. marley c. daday, leo bausing gomez, joel dingle plaza, romeo o. magadan, and virgilio a. julao, accused-appellants. iii. the revised penal code – book two > g. title vii – crimes committed by public officers **malversation (art. 217, rpc).** under the last paragraph of article 217, an accountable public officer's failure to have public funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence that the officer put them to personal use. this is a presumption of law that shifts the burden to the accused to rebut it with satisfactory evidence (reiterated, citing *wa-acon v. people*). **notwithstanding the stated purpose or intention for public funds to be applied for a public purpose, the presumption of malversation remains unrebutted absent proof that the funds were actually applied for that purpose.** a memorandum of agreement and sanggunian resolutions declaring that loans to local officials are for buying official service vehicles do not prove that the vehicles were bought and used for official purposes.

**section 3(e), ra 3019.** mere bad faith or partiality and negligence per se are not enough; the bad faith or partiality must be "evident" or "manifest" (reiterated, citing *sistoza v. desierto*). evident bad faith connotes not only bad judgment but a "palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing for some perverse motive or ill will." **local officials who, having no legal officer, acted on the opinion of the resident coa auditor that their fund realignment and loan scheme was legal did not act with evident bad faith.** they could presume the auditor performed his functions regularly and correctly, even though the opinion was verbal and given before audit. a finding that they "should have known better" shows ignorance, not evident bad faith.

charlon fernando y esma, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. vii. criminal procedure > m. new trial or reconsideration (rule 121) **for the retraction of a witness to be a ground for new trial, it must be shown that: (1) the retracting witness's trial testimony is essential to the judgment of conviction, so that its elimination would lead the trial judge to a different conclusion; (2) special circumstances exist which, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the truth of the testimony given at trial; and (3) no other evidence sustains the judgment of conviction except that testimony.** the court drew these requisites together from reyes v. people (1941, en banc) and people v. manigbas (1960, en banc). the ground is newly discovered evidence under rule 121, section 2(b): evidence discovered after trial, which could not have been discovered and produced at trial with reasonable diligence, and which is material and would probably change the judgment.

the nature of the action, and the court that has jurisdiction, are determined by the **allegations in the complaint**, not by later pleadings or motions. **a complaint that merely alleges the plaintiff's ownership and seeks to recover possession, without praying for recovery of ownership or annulment of title and without alleging that the defendant disputes the plaintiff's title, is an accion publiciana, not an accion reivindicatoria.** not every encroachment case is an accion reivindicatoria. "without claim of title" means there is no claim of title hostile to or inconsistent with the plaintiff's, or, if there is one, it is not alleged in the complaint. if ownership is raised only in the answer, the court in an accion publiciana may resolve it provisionally, and only to settle possession, where the two issues are inseparably linked.

under **rule 9, section 1** of the rules of court, a court may dismiss a claim motu proprio only for (1) lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, (2) litis pendentia, (3) res judicata, or (4) prescription. prematurity is not one of them (reiterated). iii. civil procedure > e. pleadings > 5. effect of failure to plead (rule 9, secs. 1 and 2) ii. jurisdiction > a. concept > 7. how jurisdiction is determined and conferred
01-rosario-ponencias/ac-14062-20250402:
manuel h. reyes, complainant, vs. atty. diosdado c. sebrio, jr., respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > a. legal ethics (cpra) > 9. discipline and disbarment of lawyers (canon vi) > c. charges and sanctions a lawyer who tells a client that he has friends in government offices who "will definitely offer a hand" in the client's transaction violates **canon i, section 2 and canon ii, section 15 of the cpra** (merit-based practice; improper claim of influence or familiarity). **whether the boast is true, or whether the connections are actually used, is irrelevant; the mere claim of influence consummates the offense** (reiterating *rodco consultancy v. concepcion*, decided under rule 15.06 of the cpr).

a lawyer who receives money for a specific purpose must account for it and, if it is not used for that purpose, return it promptly; failure to return it upon demand gives rise to a presumption of misappropriation (**canon iii, section 49**, the successor of rule 16.01 of the cpr). accepting payment without rendering the service violates canon ii, section 1, canon iii, section 6, and canon iv, sections 2, 3, 4, and 6. failure to pay a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct under canon ii, section 1. each of these may amount to **gross misconduct, a serious offense** under canon vi, section 33(a), punishable under section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding php 100,000.00.

when the respondent has already been disbarred, **the court keeps its jurisdiction over offenses he committed while still a lawyer.** it can no longer impose a second disbarment, but it may still declare the penalty, to be recorded in his file with the office of the bar confidant for consideration if he later petitions to lift the disbarment or seeks judicial clemency. it may also impose fines, which may be increased under canon vi, section 39 when aggravating circumstances are present (here, prior administrative liability and lack of remorse). under canon vi, section 37, **the lawyer must return money "intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship," but the court will not order payment of a personal loan from the complainant**, because a disciplinary case is not a civil action for collection (reiterating *sosa v. mendoza* and *heenan v. espejo*). the complainant may file a separate civil or criminal action.

the court **clarified** that section 4 of revised rule 140 **does not automatically make a judge liable as a lawyer** for every improper act that has a matching provision in the cpra or the lawyer's oath. the court must first ask whether the misconduct casts serious doubt on the judge's moral fitness and integrity as a member of the bar. added sanctions as a lawyer are confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character. acts that pertain to the performance of official functions (tardiness, smoking, hearing cases outside the proper court, sleeping in trial) do not qualify.
