united coconut planters bank, substituted by land bank of the philippines, petitioner, vs. editha f. ang and violeta m. fernandez, respondents. ix. special contracts > d. credit transactions > 4. real estate mortgage > b. foreclosure (rules of court, rule 68; act 3135, as amended by act 4118; ra 8791, sec. 47) **when the interest rates on a secured loan are void because the lender imposed them unilaterally (making them potestative and contrary to the mutuality of contracts under articles 1308 and 1309 of the civil code), the foreclosure that follows the borrower's non-payment is also void.** "the unilateral imposition of interests, at such rate that the lender or mortgagee so pleases, cannot and should not be reason to justify a foreclosure sale." the mortgagor must first be given the chance to pay the debt at the correct amount, at an interest rate clearly agreed upon by the parties. as the court quoted from *vasquez v. philippine national bank*: under **article 1252 of the civil code**, if a debt produces interest, payment of the principal is not deemed made until the interests have been covered; since the void interest is not demandable, the principal is not yet demandable either, so the debtor is not in default and the foreclosure should not proceed. the registration of such a foreclosure sale cannot vest title in the purchaser.

the rule **does not depend on the cause of the borrower's non-payment or on how much of the principal the borrower had paid**: as long as the interest rates were unconscionable or unilaterally imposed by the mortgagee, the foreclosure proceedings that followed should be annulled.

on reconsideration, the court **vacated its own november 24, 2021 decision**, which had relied on the statement in *advocates for truth in lending, inc. v. bangko sentral monetary board* that the right to foreclose subsists despite the nullity of usurious interest. it held instead that *spouses andal v. pnb*, *spouses albos v. spouses embisan* and *vasquez v. pnb* (which follow *heirs of espiritu v. landrito*) "should be relied upon for being more attuned to our civil laws and more in keeping with the spirit of fair play and justice," and adopted the view of justice zalameda's dissent to the original decision. viii. obligations and contracts > b. contracts > 1. general provisions > b. fundamental principles > ii. mutuality ix. special contracts > d. credit transactions > 1. loan > b. mutuum > i. interest viii. obligations and contracts > a. obligations > 5. extinguishment > a. payment or performance

"amy", accused-appellant. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640) **the failure to place seized drugs in an evidence bag or appropriate container is not automatically fatal** to a prosecution for illegal possession of dangerous drugs, because neither section 21 of r.a. no. 9165 nor the chain of custody rule requires it. the evidence bag exists to prevent switching or contamination, so "it is not so much the type or designation of the container used to store the drug evidence that matters but the manner in which said evidence was handled and transferred from one officer to another in the chain of custody." **where there is no proof that an evidence bag was used, courts look primarily at that handling and transfer, taking into account the type and amount of drugs involved and whether the circumstances warrant a different type of handling or container.** conversely, if the evidence is improperly handled or transferred, using an evidence bag will not validate its custody.

the court traced the evidence-bag requirement from the 1999 pnp drug enforcement manual to the 2015 pdea guidelines and distinguished cases where unbagged or unsealed drugs led to acquittal (tumabini, alvarado, ramos). it reiterated that a more exacting standard applies to minuscule amounts, which are more prone to tampering, while the chain of custody rule need not be applied as strictly to considerable amounts in heat-sealed packets (ramos; veloo).

people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. jeorge ejercito estregan, arlyn lazaro-torres, terryl gamit-talabong, kalahi u. rabago, erwin p. sacluti, gener c. dimaranan, and marilyn m. bruel, accused-appellants. iv. special penal laws > e. anti-graft and corrupt practices act (ra 3019, as amended by bp 195 and ra 10910) a violation of procurement laws, rules and regulations does **not per se** result in conviction under **section 3(e) of ra 3019** (reiterated). the prosecution must still prove beyond reasonable doubt that:

- the accused is a public officer discharging administrative, judicial or official functions;
- the accused acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith or gross inexcusable negligence; and
- the accused caused undue injury to any party, including the government, or gave a private party unwarranted benefits, advantage or preference.

under the second mode, the third element is met even without proof of damage. **a mayor who bypasses public bidding and contracts with an entity he knows lacks legal authority and any track record gives it unwarranted benefit with manifest partiality and evident bad faith.** the private party who conspires with him is equally liable. by contrast, **sanggunian members who merely pass an ordinance authorizing the mayor to contract with "any competent and qualified entity"** (even if it wrongly authorizes negotiated procurement) and later ratify the contract show no partiality toward a particular entity. this is especially so where the contract's validity did not depend on their resolution, which confers no rights.

an agreement by which one undertakes, for a consideration, to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability from an unknown or contingent event is a **contract of insurance** (pd 612, sec. 2(1)). a memorandum of agreement under which a firm indemnifies tourists and boatmen for accidental death or dismemberment, and reimburses the municipality's medical expenses up to scheduled amounts, is accident insurance, because indemnity is its principal object. the absence of a separately labeled premium is not conclusive. as "goods" under ra 9184, such a contract must be procured by competitive bidding unless a ground for an alternative method exists. procedurally, a sandiganbayan judgment in a criminal case within its original jurisdiction is appealed to the supreme court by **notice of appeal** (2018 revised internal rules of the sandiganbayan, rule ix, sec. 1(a)). ii. insurance law > a. general principles vii. criminal procedure > n. appeal (rule 122)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-246027-20250128:
securities and exchange commission, petitioner, vs. 1accountants party-list, inc., represented by its president, christian jay d. lim, christian jay d. lim in his personal capacity as cpa, froilan g. ampil, allan m. basarte, virgilio f. agunod, and jonas p. mascariñas, respondents. x. administrative law > c. powers of administrative agencies > 1. quasi-legislative or rulemaking power > b. requisites for validity **on the sec's second motion for reconsideration, the court en banc reversed and set aside its june 21, 2022 decision and june 27, 2023 resolution. it declared rule 68, paragraph 3 of the src irr and sec mc no. 13, s. 2009 valid and not unconstitutional. the sec may require accreditation of cpas who perform the statutory audit of the financial statements of corporations that issue registered securities and hold secondary licenses (covered entities).** the 2022 ruling that the sec lacked this authority is abandoned. the resolution opens: "the right of the state to regulate the practice of professions takes precedence over the privilege of practicing the same."

the authority rests on the following grounds:
- src sec. 5.1(d) empowers the sec to "regulate, investigate or supervise the activities of persons to ensure compliance." the law does not distinguish between natural and juridical persons, so it covers individual auditors.
- src sec. 5.1(n) and rcc sec. 179(p) grant powers implied from, or necessary or incidental to, the sec's express powers. src sec. 72 allows rules that carry out the src's provisions and purposes, chiefly investor protection. **an express grant of authority is "not a condition sine qua non" for the sec to impose an accreditation requirement.** this implied power comes from the text of the src and the rcc, not from the doctrine of necessary implication, so no gap in the law need be shown.
- rcc sec. 179(d) allows rules consistent with international best practices on corporate governance.
- rcc sec. 177 opens with "except as otherwise provided in this code or in the rules issued by the commission." this lets the sec qualify who may audit a corporation's annual financial statements.

the accreditation regulates only the activity of statutory audit of covered entities, not the accountancy profession itself. it complements, and does not replace, the licensure power of the board of accountancy. **the practice of a profession is a privilege burdened with conditions, not a right.** the professional license is a property right only in that the licensee cannot be deprived of it without due process, so accreditation is a condition on a privilege, not a curtailment of a right. the canon that a general rule-making power yields to a specific grant applies only when the two conflict. *airlift asia* was distinguished. finally, the moa between the board and the financial sector regulators is not an undue delegation of legislative power. collaboration that aligns with state policy and does not contravene a statute is a valid exercise of administrative discretion. i. business organizations > a. corporations (ra 11232) vi. special commercial laws > a. securities regulation (ra 8799)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-258710-20250127:
people of the philippines, petitioner, vs. datu akmad "tato" ampatuan, sr., respondent. ii. the revised penal code – book one > b. criminal liability > 7. participation in acts giving rise to criminal liability > b. conspiracy and proposal > i. as a mode of incurring criminal liability **to be liable as a conspirator, the accused must have performed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy, that is, an act that promotes, advances, or facilitates the progress of the plan.** the overt act may be active participation in the crime itself, or moral assistance by being present at its commission or by exerting moral ascendancy over the co-conspirators. **mere presence at the planning, and statements made in agreement with the plot, are approval or acquiescence, not acts in furtherance, and are not enough to convict**, unless the approval is so indispensable that without it the plan would not be set in motion or carried out. by contrast, offering one's guns for the killing is an overt act even if other guns were used: the act need only be done *in furtherance* of the conspiracy; it need not actually further it. a conspirator absent from the scene is liable only if it is proved that his moral ascendancy moved the others to carry out the plan. moral ascendancy cannot be presumed from kinship or public position.

**a judgment of acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory** (finality-of-acquittal rule, which shares the purpose of the right against double jeopardy). it may be challenged only by certiorari for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, as where the prosecution was denied the opportunity to present its case or the trial was a sham. gross misapprehension of facts is not by itself an exception to double jeopardy. it establishes grave abuse only if it is patent and gross and was exercised in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner, because "[w]himsicality, not accuracy, is the core of certiorari proceedings."

under **article 20 of the rpc**, one who would otherwise be an accessory is exempt when the principal is a relative within the degrees stated, including relatives by affinity within the same degrees (here, the son-in-law of a principal). vii. criminal procedure > i. motion to quash (rule 117) > 2. double jeopardy viii. constitutional rights > s. right against double jeopardy
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-248842-20250122:
vilma b. cabrera, petitioner, vs. the honorable office of the ombudsman, public assistance and corruption prevention office (pacpo) of the office of the ombudsman, respondents. xi. law on public officers > d. accountability of public officers (ra 6713) > 2. discipline > a. grounds **reiterated definitions.** *grave misconduct* is the transgression of an established rule, particularly unlawful behavior or gross negligence by a public officer, coupled with corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. without these elements, the offense is only simple misconduct. *dishonesty* is the concealment or distortion of truth in a matter relevant to one's office. it is a question of intention, judged from the officer's conduct and outward acts. *conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service* covers acts that tarnish the image and integrity of the public office, even if they are not related to the officer's functions. each must be proved by substantial evidence. the ombudsman's factual findings, when supported by substantial evidence, are conclusive and given great weight.

**a public officer who recommends and certifies the release of pdaf funds to an ngo in disregard of mandatory dswd and coa circulars is liable for grave misconduct, serious dishonesty and conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service.** the circulars must be read as a whole. a registered ngo becomes eligible for a pdaf transfer only after the dswd legislative liaison office (dllo) determines its eligibility through an endorsement from the standards bureau, and ngos that have not liquidated earlier releases are ineligible. these circulars are mandatory, are meant to secure full accountability for public funds, and "could not just be disregarded by mere practice."

a head of office cannot disown certifications signed **"for" her** by an officer-in-charge by claiming that the oic acted as her substitute. she should have reviewed documents signed on her behalf, especially those involving the release of public funds. viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 1. standards > c. substantial evidence

godofredo v. arquiza, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. iii. the revised penal code – book two > m. title xiii – crimes against honor utterances made in judicial or administrative proceedings are **absolutely privileged**, whatever their defamatory tenor and even if made with malice, as long as they are relevant, pertinent, or material to the cause or inquiry (reiterated). the privilege also covers preliminary investigations and other steps preparatory to trial (reiterated, alcantara v. ponce; belen v. people).

**new rule: absolute privilege extends to statements made in quasi-judicial proceedings, including steps necessarily preliminary to them.** relevancy is the lone test for judicial proceedings. for quasi-judicial proceedings, the court laid down a **four-fold test**:
- **quasi-judicial powers test:** was the document containing the alleged defamatory statement filed or submitted as a necessarily preliminary step to, or during, a quasi-judicial proceeding?
- **safeguards test:** does the proceeding afford procedural protections similar to those of the judicial process (notice, opportunity to be heard and to controvert charges, to submit evidence, to cross-examine, and an objective decision-maker)?
- **relevancy test:** was the statement relevant and pertinent to the proceeding? doubts are resolved liberally in favor of relevancy.
- **non-publication test:** did the author communicate the document only to those who have a duty to perform with respect to it and to those legally required to be served a copy?

applying the test, allegations in a **petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of nomination of party-list nominees** filed with the comelec (comelec resolution no. 9366) are absolutely privileged. that petition invokes the comelec's quasi-judicial function and its summary proceedings keep notice, hearing, evidence, and cross-examination. charging the nominee with a "criminal bent" and being a "fugitive from justice" is relevant because those are the very grounds for cancellation. furnishing copies to the impleaded respondents, as the resolution requires, is not publication. xii. election law > e. remedies and jurisdiction > 2. petition to deny due course or cancel certificate of nomination of party-list nominees (cr 9366, rule 5) iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > e. modes > v. appeal by certiorari to sc (rule 45)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-249832-20241113:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. monico badillo, accused-appellant. ii. the revised penal code – book one > b. criminal liability > 8. circumstances affecting criminal liability > d. aggravating circumstances **treachery cannot be appreciated when no witness saw how the attack began.** there is treachery when (1) the means of execution gave the person attacked no opportunity to defend himself or retaliate, and (2) those means were deliberately or consciously adopted (*people v. corpin*). a "sudden" and "unexpected" attack is not enough by itself: the prosecution must show that the offender purposely adopted that mode of attack to ensure its execution without risk to himself. treachery must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, as conclusively as the killing itself. it cannot rest on conjecture, and when there is no precise evidence of how the attack commenced, the doubt is resolved in favor of the accused. without treachery, the killing is homicide under article 249 of the rpc. reiterated.

appeals in criminal cases to the supreme court are generally by petition for review on certiorari under rule 45 (rule 122, sec. 3(e)). a notice of appeal filed with the ca is the mode under rule 124, sec. 13(c). where the ca downgraded murder to homicide and imposed *reclusion temporal*, the court held that the accused's notice of appeal was the wrong remedy. it nonetheless treated the appeal as a rule 45 petition in the interest of substantial justice. even under rule 45, an appeal in a criminal case throws the whole case open for review, because guilt is essentially a question of fact.

also reiterated:
- the trial court's assessment of the witnesses' credibility is accorded great weight.
- minor inconsistencies (where in the house the victim was stabbed, how many times) and a two-month delay in reporting the crime do not impair credibility.
- denial and alibi cannot prevail over positive identification by credible witnesses with no ill motive. alibi requires proof of physical impossibility and is weakened when corroborated only by relatives.
- for homicide, the court awarded php 50,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and temperate damages (*people v. jugueta*), deleted the exemplary damages, and sustained attorney's fees under article 2208. vii. criminal procedure > n. appeal (rule 122) xii. damages > c. other kinds of damages > 3. temperate or moderate damages
01-rosario-ponencias/ac-11889-20241113:
re: resolution dated august 30, 2017 in omb-c-c-13-0357, etc., complainant, vs. atty. editha p. talaboc, atty. delfin r. agcaoili, jr., and atty. mark s. oliveros, respondents. ix. legal and judicial ethics > a. legal ethics (cpra) > 9. discipline and disbarment of lawyers (canon vi) > e. burden of proof and quantum of evidence **in disciplinary proceedings, the lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed his or her duties in accordance with the oath; the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence** (rule 133, sec. 6 of the rules on evidence). mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions are not proof, and the respondent's failure to answer the complaint is not an admission of its allegations (reiterated).

a notary public is **not liable** for notarizations made in his or her name where there is substantial evidence that the signatures were forged and the notarial certificates themselves are irregular (missing the commission serial number, office address, ibp chapter or place of issue of the ptr; commission periods and ibp/ptr receipts that do not match official records), casting doubt on the validity of the seals and stamps used. negligence in safekeeping the notarial paraphernalia cannot then be inferred: "notaries are not immune from identity theft." the court distinguished *rigon v. atty. subia* (notary accountable for his seal where he did not deny its authenticity) and cases where negligence was shown by giving secretaries full access to the notarial paraphernalia or by entries in the notarial books. given the proliferation of fake notaries, liability for alleged violations of the notarial rules is determined **case by case**.

separately, **failing to comply with the ibp-cbd's directives** (to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper) **violates canon iii, sec. 2 of the cpra** and is a **less serious offense under canon vi, sec. 34(c)**, sanctioned under sec. 37(b). a first offense is mitigating (sec. 38(a)(1)), allowing a fine of not less than half the minimum (php 17,500.00) under sec. 39; previous administrative liability is aggravating, allowing a penalty up to double the maximum.
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-259520-20241105:
maria lina p. quirit-figarido, petitioner, vs. edwin l. figarido, respondent. iii. family relations > a. marriage > 4. void and voidable marriages **only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may file a petition to declare a bigamous marriage void. the spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage has no personality to file it.** bigamous marriages are void ab initio under article 35(4) of the family code. but under section 2(a) of a.m. no. 02-11-10-sc, a petition for declaration of absolute nullity "may be filed solely by the husband or the wife," and the rationale of the rule explains that "[o]nly an aggrieved or injured spouse" may file. following *juliano-llave v. republic* and *fujiki v. marinay*, the "husband or the wife" means the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage are neither husband nor wife in law. the en banc applied these rules and jurisprudence to deny standing to the guilty spouse. letting her sue would be a "legal absurdity": the offending spouse could dissolve the marriage at will and treat bigamy "as a matter of convenience."

a foreign divorce later obtained by the prior spouse ends that spouse's standing, since there is no longer a prior subsisting marriage. but it **does not pass the right to sue to the guilty spouse.** when the persons capable of filing are absent or disqualified, other parties do not automatically gain the right to attack the bigamous marriage. the state has no absolute duty to dissolve bigamous marriages, and the court will not use its equity jurisdiction to free a party who willfully entered the void marriage and does not come with clean hands (*alcantara v. alcantara*).

the denial does not legalize the bigamous marriage. under article 40 of the family code, a judicial declaration of nullity is needed only for purposes of remarriage. for other purposes, such as heirship, legitimacy or illegitimacy of a child, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, or a criminal case, a court may rule on the marriage's validity in any case where the question is essential (*cariño v. cariño*). the erring parties also remain civilly and criminally liable for bigamy. iii. civil procedure > c. parties to civil actions (rule 3)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-261113-20241104:
hilario cosme y terenal, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. iv. special penal laws > v. comprehensive firearms and ammunition regulation act (ra 10591, secs. 3 and 28–41) in illegal possession of firearms under **sec. 28(a) of ra 10591**, possession per se is not prohibited; the corpus delicti is the accused's **lack of a license or permit** to possess or carry the firearm. the prosecution must prove (a) the existence of the firearm and (b) that the accused who owned or possessed it has no corresponding license **or permit**. a non-licensee may carry a firearm under a permit sanctioned by law, such as a **duty detail order (ddo)**, which under the 2018 revised irr of ra 10591 is the security personnel's authority to carry the issued firearm within the specific duration and location of the posting.

**licensed private security professionals (psps) derive their authority to carry their service firearm from the ddo itself, not from the employer's license, and are entitled to presume that their agency issued them a licensed firearm** (applying *cuenca v. people* under ra 10591). hence, even if the firearm turns out to be unlicensed, no criminal liability attaches absent proof that the accused freely and voluntarily possessed it knowing it to be unlicensed. the psp must be licensed to exercise the profession and must possess the firearm within the premises and period specified in the ddo. errors or omissions in the ddo are the agency's responsibility, and the same presumption covers ammunition appropriate to the firearm.

**clarified:** the statement in *people v. de gracia* that good faith is no defense applies only where the accused had no license or authority in the first place. **where the accused has proper authority, possession of the firearm under a good-faith belief that it is licensed is a valid defense.** failure to carry the ddo or to wear the prescribed uniform while on duty may result in administrative liability, not criminal liability.
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-226859-20241104:
perlita rodriguez, petitioner, vs. laura elorde, respondent. ii. the revised penal code – book one > d. extinction of criminal liability > 1. total extinction > a. death of convict **the death of the accused before final judgment totally extinguishes criminal liability under article 89(1) of the rpc.** when the accused dies while her petition questioning the reinstatement of the criminal case against her is pending, the petition becomes moot and academic, and the court dismisses the criminal case itself, "inasmuch as there is no longer a defendant to stand as the accused therein" (reiterated).

the effects on civil liability, as summarized in *people v. culas* and *people v. monroyo* (reiterated): (1) death extinguishes the criminal liability and the civil liability based solely on the offense (civil liability *ex delicto* in the strict sense); (2) civil liability survives if it may also be based on another source of obligation under article 1157 of the civil code (law, contracts, quasi-contracts, quasi-delicts); (3) the surviving claim may be pursued only through a separate civil action, subject to section 1, rule 111, against the executor/administrator or the estate, depending on the source of the obligation; and (4) if the civil action was instituted together with the criminal action, the statute of limitations on the civil liability is deemed interrupted while the criminal case was pending (art. 1155, civil code).

reiterated (*people v. ramoy*): **an order denying a motion to quash is interlocutory, not appealable, and generally not subject to certiorari.** the accused must enter a plea, go to trial, and, if the judgment is adverse, assign the denial as error on appeal. immediate resort to certiorari is allowed only for special or exceptional reasons. vii. criminal procedure > i. motion to quash (rule 117) vii. criminal procedure > c. prosecution of civil action (rule 111) > 4. civil liability ex delicto > b. when accused dies
01-rosario-ponencias/oca-ipi-18-4887-rtj:
maria magdalena r. joven, complainant, vs. hon. monique a. quisumbing-ignacio, presiding judge, branch 209, regional trial court, mandaluyong city, victor m. pe benito, sheriff iv, and alfredo marcelo bermejo, administrative aide iv, all of branch 209, regional trial court, mandaluyong city, respondents. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 2. accountability of members of the judiciary > a. judicial accountability and disciplinary proceedings (canon vii) reiterated: **an administrative complaint is not the appropriate remedy for every act of a judge deemed aberrant or irregular where a judicial remedy exists and is available.** acts of a judge in his or her judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action; a judge cannot be held civilly, criminally or administratively liable for official acts, "no matter how erroneous," provided he or she acted in good faith (*biado v. brawner-cualing*). disciplinary proceedings do not complement, supplement or substitute judicial remedies, and an inquiry into administrative liability arising from judicial acts may be made only after the other available remedies have been settled (*bello iii v. diaz*). charges that are judicial in nature must be raised through the proper judicial action, not an administrative complaint (*ala v. peras*).

the complainant must prove the charges by **substantial evidence**. **bad faith and malice cannot be presumed just because the judge's order is adverse to the complainant.** to hold a judge liable for deliberately rendering an unjust order, the complainant must show that the order is unjust and that it was issued with malicious intent to cause injustice; bare allegations, conjectures and speculations do not suffice. a sheriff who merely serves a writ and an order of the court performs a ministerial duty.
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-259982-20241028:
pacific ocean manning, inc. and/or v. ships uk ltd./nordic american tankers limited, petitioners, vs. nicolas f. bobiles, respondent. vii. social legislation > d. disability and death benefits > 2. seafarers (ra 12021, secs. 22, 28–29, 32, 57, and its irr; 2010 poea standard employment contract) **the court clarified the rules on attorney's fees in worker disability and death indemnification cases:**

- **article 111 of the labor code** (attorney's fees of 10% of the wages recovered) applies **only to cases of unlawful withholding of wages**. it does not apply to claims involving only disability or death benefits. the statement in heirs of aniban v. nlrc that article 111 is not limited to withheld wages is "inaccurate"; article 111 sits under the labor code chapter on "payment of wages."
- **article 2208(2) of the civil code** (defendant's act compelled the plaintiff "to litigate with third persons or to incur expenses to protect [their] interest") applies **only when the litigation or expense is in relation to third persons**, not the defendant itself (the "wrongful act doctrine"). the litigation with third persons may be in the same suit. it must be the natural and proximate consequence of the defendant's wrongful act and be incurred necessarily and in good faith. being compelled to sue the defendant itself is not enough; otherwise attorney's fees would become the rule rather than the exception, and a premium would be placed on the right to litigate.
- **article 2208(8)** (actions for indemnity under workmen's compensation and employer's liability laws) applies only to actions under those laws, now title ii, book iv of the labor code on employees' compensation. it **does not apply to disability claims based on contract, such as the poea-sec.**
- an award under the catch-all **article 2208(11)** requires a factual, legal, or equitable justification.

on disability benefits (reiterated): the company-designated physician must issue a final assessment within 120 days, extendible to 240 days only with sufficient justification, which the employer must prove (elburg shipmanagement v. quiogue). **an assessment is not final when the physician, on the same date, finds that the seafarer still needs treatment or re-evaluation** (benhur shipping v. riego). without a valid, final, and definite assessment within the period, the law deems the disability total and permanent, and the seafarer need not go through the third-doctor referral under the poea-sec. xii. damages > b. actual and compensatory damages > 4. attorney's fees and expenses of litigation
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-261123-20240820:
duty to energize the republic through the enlightenment of the youth [duterte youth] party-list, represented by [chairperson] ronald gian carlo l. cardema and representative ducielle marie s. cardema, petitioner, vs. commission on elections, house of representatives, komunidad ng pamilya, pasyente at persons with disabilities [p3pwd] party-list and its nominees led by rowena amelia v. guanzon, respondents. [g.r. no. 261876] duty to energize the republic through the enlightenment of the youth [duterte youth] party-list, represented by [chairperson] ronald gian carlo l. cardema and representative ducielle marie s. cardema, petitioner, vs. ma. rowena amelia v. guanzon, respondent. xii. election law > c. political parties and the party-list system of representation > 2. qualifications, nomination, and substitution of party-list nominees and representatives **rules and regulations limiting the substitution of party-list nominees are matters of substance, not form, so they do not lose their mandatory character even after the elections.** the doctrine that election rules are mandatory before the elections but directory after them (engle v. comelec, citing mitra v. comelec) applies only to matters of form. the timing of substitution affects the electorate's right to know who a party-list's nominees are (lokin; cocofed; bantay republic act). the comelec gravely abuses its discretion when, after the elections and beyond its own deadline, it hastily approves the en masse substitution of all of a winning party-list's nominees. such approval is void.

other key rules the court laid down or reiterated:
- **section 8 vs. section 16 of ra 7941.** section 8 (no change of names or order of nominees after submission, except when a nominee dies, withdraws in writing, or becomes incapacitated; the substitute is placed last) and its implementing comelec resolutions govern substitutions before the term starts. section 16 (a vacancy is filled automatically by the next nominee; additional nominees are submitted once the list is exhausted) applies only to a vacancy in a party-list **seat**, which legally exists only during the term, from noon of june 30 after the election. it does not apply to a vacancy in the list.
- **withdrawal.** ra 7941 does not prohibit the withdrawal of a nominee, whatever the reason and whether before, during, or after the elections. the comelec may neither grant nor deny a withdrawal; it merely notes it.
- **comelec rule-making.** even though ra 7941 sets no deadline for substitution, the comelec may validly impose one (res. no. 9366, as amended by res. no. 10690) under section 18 of ra 7941. the deadline is germane to the law's purposes and supplants no express provision, unlike the added ground for withdrawal struck down in lokin or the statutory deadline moved in pdp-laban.
- **administrative function, voting, remedy.** approving a substitution, and resolving an opposition that needs only the application of laws and rules, is an administrative function. an opposition or a question of fact does not by itself make the proceeding quasi-judicial (aggabao distinguished). so the comelec en banc may act directly. article ix-a, section 7 of the constitution (majority of all members) does not apply; a vote of a majority of the commissioners present at a meeting with a quorum (sec. 2, comelec res. no. 9936) suffices. review is by certiorari under rule 65, not rule 64.
- **standing.** taxpayer, voter, citizen, and legislator suits still require a claim of injury-in-fact. voters may challenge any rule, regulation, or ruling that injures their rights as voters, not only election laws. citizens have standing in a case of transcendental importance anchored on the right to information on matters of public concern (akbayan).
- **tro and hret jurisdiction.** the rule that the fallo prevails applies only when it conflicts with the body, not when it merely omits something; an order is read as a whole. a tro preserves the status quo ante and stays the legal effects of a proclamation and oath, so the nominee does not assume office and jurisdiction stays with the comelec, not the hret.

**contempt (reiterated).** indirect contempt is criminal in nature: it requires proof beyond reasonable doubt and contumacious intent, and out-of-court comments on a pending case are punished under the sub judice rule (rule 71, sec. 3(d)) only if they pose a clear and present danger to the administration of justice. a person cannot be held in contempt for disobeying an order not addressed to them. a party-initiated charge requires a verified petition (rule 71, sec. 4), not a countercharge in a compliance. a lawyer who comments on a pending case to sway public perception, or who spreads false claims on social media, still answers to canon ii of the cpra (secs. 19 and 38). v. special civil actions > e. certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus (rule 65) v. special civil actions > k. contempt (rule 71) > 1. direct vs. indirect contempt ix. legal and judicial ethics > a. legal ethics (cpra) > 8. duties and responsibilities of lawyers (cpra) > c. propriety (canon ii) > i. responsible use of social media
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-252124-20240723:
bohol wisdom school, dr. simplicio yap, jr., and raul h. deloso, petitioners, vs. miraflor mabao, respondent. vi. suspension and termination of employment > a. termination or suspension by employer > 2. just causes (do 147, s. 2015) **whether an employee's conduct is disgraceful or immoral is judged by public and secular morality, not religious morality.** reiterating leus v. st. scholastica's college westgrove and inocente v. st. vincent foundation, the court held that **sexual relations between two consenting adults with no legal impediment to marry, even if they result in pregnancy out of wedlock, are not disgraceful or immoral.** no law proscribes them, and they contravene no fundamental state policy in the constitution. a sectarian school therefore cannot validly suspend a teacher for "immorality" because she became pregnant by her boyfriend before marriage, even if the conduct violates the school's religious standards. such a suspension is illegal.

a suspension must also satisfy due process. it must rest on a just or authorized cause under the labor code, and the employee must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the penalty is decided. there is no "substantial compliance" where no notice to explain was issued and the employer had decided the penalty before hearing the employee.

abandonment requires (1) failure to report for work or absence without valid or justifiable reason, and (2) a clear intention to sever the employer-employee relationship shown by an overt act. an employee who refuses return-to-work notices after her suspension ends and writes that she "could no longer go back to work for the school" abandons her employment as of that letter, and her money claims accrue only up to that date. iii. civil procedure > s. post-judgment remedies > 5. appeal and review > e. modes > v. appeal by certiorari to sc (rule 45)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-246787-20240130:
spouses enrique llonillo and marites llonillo, petitioners, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. vii. criminal procedure > c. prosecution of civil action (rule 111) > 4. civil liability ex delicto > a. when accused is acquitted **civil liability arising from a source other than the delict (law, contract, quasi-contract or quasi-delict under article 1157 of the civil code) may be adjudged in the same criminal action even if the accused is acquitted**, despite the limitation in rule 111, section 1(a) of the rules of court, and without violating due process. "for uniformity," the court **laid down new parameters**: the award may be made in the criminal action subject to the following conditions:

- (1) the act or omission complained of in the criminal action is the same as or is related to the act or omission giving rise to the civil liability;
- (2) the civil liability of the accused was raised in the criminal action;
- (3) the accused was given the opportunity to be heard on this point; and
- (4) the civil liability of the accused was established by a preponderance of evidence.

the court based this on article 29 of the civil code and rule 120, section 2 (a judgment of acquittal "shall determine if the act or omission from which the civil liability might arise did not exist"), and **reaffirmed the en banc ruling in *padilla v. court of appeals*** that courts may adjudge civil liability in the same criminal case where the acquittal is pronounced. division rulings holding otherwise cannot overturn an en banc doctrine (article viii, section 4(3), constitution). because the civil action is deemed instituted with the criminal action, the accused is expected to present there all defenses on the civil aspect.

reiterated: (a) **other deceits under article 318, paragraph 1 of the rpc** requires a false pretense or fraudulent act made **prior to or simultaneously with** the fraud, which must be the very cause or only motive for the offended party to part with his property. there is no fraudulent concealment of a mortgage that the lender admitted seeing annotated on the titles, and acts done after the transaction cannot supply the deceit. 01-rosario-ponencias/gr-220087-20231113:
hacienda san isidro/silos farms and rey silos llamado, petitioners, vs. lucito villaruel and helen villaruel, respondents. iii. employment relationship > c. kinds of employment > 5. seasonal **a seasonal employee becomes a regular employee when (1) the employee performs work or services that are seasonal in nature and (2) is employed to perform such work or services for more than one season.** the court deduced these requisites from earlier cases and stated them "for the guidance of the bench and the bar." under the first paragraph of art. 295 (formerly art. 280) of the labor code, the seasonal exception covers only employment "for the duration of the season," i.e., one season. a seasonal employee rehired for more than one season falls back under the general rule of regular employment. **the basis of regular seasonal status is this first paragraph, not the proviso of the second paragraph** (at least one year of service, continuous or broken). that proviso applies only to casual employees, i.e., those not covered by the first paragraph (*paz v. northern tobacco redrying co.*; *mercado*). the ca erred in treating the worker as a casual employee who became regular through the proviso.

freedom to offer one's services to other farm owners does not negate regular status, as long as the worker is hired repeatedly for the same activities and not merely on and off for any single phase of agricultural work. *mercado v. nlrc* was distinguished, as explained in *hacienda fatima*. pakyaw is a method of paying wages, not the relationship itself. pakyaw workers are regular employees if they are subject to the employer's control, and the control test requires only the existence of the right to control, not its actual exercise (reiterated from *gapayao v. fulo*).

kilusan ng mamamayan para sa matuwid na bayan, a coalition of corporate entities duly registered with the securities and exchange commission, which are petitioners herein as well, namely, capitol christian leadership; buklod pamilya incorporated; kmp, koalisyong pangkaunlaran ng mamamayan; and knk, anak ng diyos kadugo ni kristo, and jose lagunsad gonzales, vicente alejo macatangay, jr., sharon faith samaco paquiz, nelson java celis, melchor gruela magdamo, rodrigo g. cornejo, and melanio lazo mauricio, jr., petitioners, vs. commission on elections (comelec), respondent. v. special civil actions > e. certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus (rule 65) a petition for mandamus filed with the supreme court must carry proof of service on the adverse party (rule 56, sec. 2(c), in relation to rule 13, sec. 17) and a proper verification and certification against forum shopping (rule 65 in relation to rule 7, secs. 4 and 5). the affiant's competent evidence of identity must appear in the notarized verification and the affidavit of service (2004 rules on notarial practice, rule ii, secs. 2, 6 and 12). **parties who did not execute the verification and certification, including organizations with no authorized representative, are dropped as petitioners. where the remaining petitioners still fail to cure the defects after the court ordered compliance, the petition is dismissed.** id copies attached at the end of the compliance do not cure a verification whose face does not show the affiants' competent evidence of identity. that the ids were shown to the notary is "a mere speculation."

**when a party is required during pre-trial or discovery to disclose all evidence supporting its assertions, it must produce such evidence; otherwise, all evidence existing but not so disclosed is considered intentionally concealed and is denied admission when formally offered** (reiterating g.r. no. 188881). this applies where the party repeatedly manifested that it had no more documents to produce and later offered undisclosed documents without a plausible explanation. photocopies and unauthenticated documents are likewise excluded under the best evidence rule.

a civil suit to recover unlawfully acquired property under ra 1379, or for restitution, reparation or damages, against the marcoses and their associates, dummies, agents and nominees **is civil in nature and is proved by a preponderance of evidence** (e.o. no. 14-a, sec. 3). the plaintiff's evidence must tend to prove the allegations of its complaint; evidence that requires "many leaps of logic" and inferences upon inferences reduces the allegations to speculation and warrants dismissal.

marilou casas usama, complainant, vs. (ret.) hon. oscar d. tomarong, branch 28, regional trial court, liloy, zamboanga del norte, respondent. ix. legal and judicial ethics > b. judicial ethics (cjca) > 2. accountability of members of the judiciary > a. judicial accountability and disciplinary proceedings (canon vii) **in all cases, whether bail is a matter of right or of discretion, the judge must notify the prosecutor of the bail application or require his recommendation. where bail is discretionary (offenses punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment), the judge must hold a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong** (const., art. iii, sec. 13; rule 114, secs. 7, 8, and 18; oca v. judge flor, jr.; villanueva v. judge buaya, which requires notice and hearing even when bail is a matter of right, to apply the section 9 guidelines in fixing the amount). the judge's own view that the killing was "only homicide," and the fact that no information had yet been filed, do not excuse notice and hearing. a judge who grants bail on the day it is filed without either commits **gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct**. a petition for habeas corpus is not the proper vehicle to assert a right to bail (galvez v. ca), and ordering the release on bail of persons who are not parties to the habeas corpus case is a separate act of gross ignorance and gross misconduct.

equitable pcibank, petitioner, vs. spouses maximo and soledad lacson and marietta f. yuching, respondents. xii. damages > b. actual and compensatory damages > 1. concept actual or compensatory damages (art. 2199, civil code) compensate for a pecuniary loss actually sustained. they **cannot be presumed**: the claimant must prove (1) the fact of injury or loss and (2) the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty, by competent proof and the best evidence obtainable (reiterated). **a bank that dishonors a depositor's checks drawn against insufficient funds or a closed account suffers no actual loss equal to their face value.** no collection is made and nothing is charged against the bank; the money never leaves its ledger and custody. even if check kiting is proved, the bank must still prove that it suffered injury as a result.

the court observed that in a kiting scheme the bank's actual damage could instead take the form of **interest on the amounts credited to the kiting accounts**, from crediting until discovery or reversal. during that time the depositor used the bank's credit, so the amount is treated as borrowed and the depositor answers for its time value. such interest must be claimed and proved.

**exemplary damages** (art. 2229) are awarded only in addition to moral, temperate, liquidated, or compensatory damages. they are not a matter of right. the claimant must first establish a right to one of those damages, and the wrongful act must be accompanied by bad faith, done in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent manner. without compensatory damages, exemplary damages cannot be awarded. absent a stipulation, **attorney's fees** (art. 2208) are recoverable only in the cases the law allows, such as when exemplary damages are awarded, so they fall with the exemplary damages (reiterated). viii. evidence > d. weight and sufficiency (rule 133) > 1. standards > b. preponderance of evidence

mario nisperos y padilla, petitioner, vs. people of the philippines, respondent. iii. the revised penal code – book two > e. title v – crimes relative to opium and other prohibited drugs > 1. repealed. see instead comprehensive dangerous drugs act of 2002 (ra 9165, art. ii, as amended by ra 10640; see also am 18-03-16-sc) in buy-bust operations (warrantless arrests), the insulating witnesses required by **section 21(1) of ra 9165, as amended by ra 10640, must be present "at or near" the place of apprehension**, so that the inventory and photographing can be done "immediately after seizure and confiscation." since they may be "near" and not necessarily "at" the place, **they need not witness the arrest or the seizure itself; they only need to be readily available to witness the immediately ensuing inventory.** the en banc thus clarified the statement in *people v. tomawis* that the witnesses' presence must be secured at the time of the warrantless arrest. **the late arrival of a required witness is not a justifiable ground for delaying the inventory**; the buy-bust team must ensure that all witnesses are readily available.

bureau of customs employees association (bocea), represented by its national president mr. romulo a. pagulayan, petitioner, vs. hon. rozzano rufino b. biazon (in his capacity as commissioner, bureau of customs), hon. cesar v. purisima (in his capacity as secretary of finance), hon. mar a. roxas (in his capacity as former secretary of the department of transportation and communications), hon. joseph emilio a. abaya (in his capacity as incumbent secretary of the department of transportation and communications), respondents. x. administrative law > c. powers of administrative agencies > 1. quasi-legislative or rulemaking power > b. requisites for validity **a petition for certiorari and prohibition under the court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction (const., art. viii, sec. 1, par. 2) is a proper remedy to question quasi-legislative acts** of executive officials, such as administrative orders, memoranda, and circulars. it remains subject to the **hierarchy of courts** (the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction, here the ca, unless the higher court grants an exemption) and to **exhaustion of administrative remedies**, which applies whether the assailed act is quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, or purely regulatory, and which is how ripeness shows itself in the case of administrative acts (reiterating *association of medical clinics for overseas workers v. gcc approved medical centers association*). the court may relax these rules, as it did here, because the overtime pay of customs employees had long been debated and repeatedly litigated.

01-rosario-ponencias/ac-13118-20220628:

national housing authority (nha), represented herein by its general manager, marcelino p. escalada, jr., froilan r. kampitan, elvira a. sabado, wilma d. hernandez, fe p. valenzuela, prudencia b. gugol, raymond n. abad, jeanette i. baccay, danilo gonzales, alejandro a. nuevas, evelyn balais, avelina lleva, ma. melani abasola, and all rank-and-file employees of nha, represented herein by evangeline a. javier, president of the consolidated union of employees of nha (cue), petitioners, vs. the commission on audit, represented by michael g. aguinaldo, in his capacity as the chairperson; mary s. adelino, in her capacity as director, cluster ii-corporate government sector of the commission on audit; janet b. reyes, in her capacity as audit team leader; and rebecca a. dumaguit, in her capacity as supervising auditor, respondents. 01-rosario-ponencias/gr-221823-20220621:
rep. nicasio m. aliping, jr., petitioner, vs. court of appeals (former 4th division), bishop carlito j. cenzon, archbishop socrates b. villegas, sheree m. nolasco, marie a. balangue, nonnette c. bennett, dr. teresita f. de venecia, antonio j. supremido, jr., and pastor gener tandoc, respondents. viii. constitutional rights > b. equal protection **a directive in a writ of kalikasan judgment that permanently enjoins only the impleaded respondent from developing his claim within a forest reserve does not violate the equal protection clause.** this holds even if other residents and garden owners in the reserve are not similarly restrained, where the directive is a specific remedial response to an anthropogenic activity unique to him and proven to be a major contributor to the environmental damage. the others are not similarly situated: they were not impleaded, and they were neither accused nor proven to have engaged in comparable acts. applying *people v. dela piedra* by analogy, unequal application is not a denial of equal protection unless there is an element of **intentional or purposeful discrimination**. a discriminatory purpose is not presumed; there must be a showing of "clear and intentional discrimination."

lily c. lopez, petitioner, vs. lolito s. lopez, ma. rachel nicolette lopez, barbara villas, benedicto villafuerte, ma. luisa paras, ruel villacorta, teresita c. fernando, and i specialist development corporation, respondents. lolito s. lopez, mario s. lopez, andresito s. lopez, barbara o. villas, benedicto l. villafuerte, ma. luisa i. paras, ruel s. villacorta, teresita c. fernando, lc lopez resources, inc., and conqueror international, inc., respondents. i. business organizations > a. corporations (ra 11232) > 6. directors and trustees > a. repository of corporate powers **corporate powers are exercised, all business conducted, and all corporate property controlled by the board of directors** (section 23, corporation code). a corporate president, even one who is a majority stockholder, cannot validly buy the corporation's unissued shares without a board resolution authorizing the sale. **the sale is invalid, and the shares cannot be voted** in electing directors. a sale of unissued shares made without first offering them to the other stockholders also violates their **preemptive right** (section 39, corporation code). a stockholders' meeting where the shares represented are less than one-half plus one of the outstanding shares lacks a quorum and is void, together with the election held at it.

on procedure, a branch clerk of court's certification that counsel, through a messenger, received the decision on a stated date enjoys the **presumption of regularity**, which only clear and convincing evidence can overcome; the burden is on the party disputing receipt. a petition for review filed beyond the 15-day period under a.m. no. 04-9-07-sc must be dismissed, because perfecting an appeal within the period is jurisdictional. antonio r. cruz and loreto teresita cruz-dimayacyac, as heirs of the late spouses dr. progedio r. cruz and teresa reyes, petitioners, vs. carling cervantes and celia cervantes santos and all persons claiming rights under them, respondents. v. special civil actions > j. forcible entry and unlawful detainer (rule 70) under **section 50-a of ra no. 6657, as added by section 19 of ra no. 9700**, the judge or prosecutor must automatically refer a case to the dar when two requisites concur: (1) an allegation from any one or both parties that the case is agrarian in nature; and (2) one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant. a mere allegation suffices for the first requisite, but the second must be proved (reiterating *chailese development co. v. dizon* and *dayrit v. norquillas*). the court **clarified** that the proof required for the second requisite is **any kind of evidence which, on its face, shows that one of the parties is a farmer, farmworker, or tenant**; a facial assessment is enough, so that the referral mechanism is not defeated by protracted proceedings in the referring court.

people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. carlos racadio asuncion, mamelfa r. amongol, genoveva r. ragasa, rosita r. ragunjan, and virginia r. rafanan, accused-appellants. iv. special penal laws > e. anti-graft and corrupt practices act (ra 3019, as amended by bp 195 and ra 10910) to convict under **sec. 3(e) of ra 3019**, the prosecution must prove that the public officer acted through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. **an erroneous interpretation of a provision of law, absent any dishonest or wrongful purpose, is not bad faith** (reiterating *ysidoro v. leonardo-de castro*); bad faith must be *evident*, partaking of fraud and showing a manifest deliberate intent to do wrong or cause damage. manifest partiality requires a clear, notorious or plain inclination to favor one side over another, and gross inexcusable negligence is negated where the officer relied on sanggunian accreditations, resolutions and appropriation ordinances. repayment of the amounts upon coa disallowance is a badge of good faith.

01-rosario-ponencias/gr-250867-20220316:
people of the philippines, plaintiff-appellee, vs. ronald n. ricketts, cyrus paul s. valenzuela, manuel j. mangubat, joseph d. arnaldo, and glenn s. perez, accused, ronald n. ricketts and glenn s. perez, accused-appellants. iv. special penal laws > e. anti-graft and corrupt practices act (ra 3019, as amended by bp 195 and ra 10910) **under the doctrine of independently relevant statements, a witness's testimony that a third person told him something is admissible only to prove that the statement was made, not that it is true;** as to the truth of what was said, it remains hearsay. a security guard's report that the accused employee, caught removing seized items, said that the "chairman" ordered the removal proves the employee's unauthorized act and that he made the statement. it does not prove that the chairman gave the order (reiterated, citing xxx v. people and gubaton v. amador).

01-rosario-ponencias/gr-249563-20220309:
encarnacion go, petitioner, vs. the people of the philippines, respondent. vii. criminal procedure > b. prosecution of offenses (rule 110) > 6. complaint or information > b. sufficiency > iii. cause of the accusation **an accused who is charged in the information as a direct participant in the offense cannot be convicted on the theory that she is liable as an officer, director, treasurer, owner, or operator of the corporation or vessel that committed it, if the information does not allege that capacity.** such a conviction violates the constitutional right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation. every element of the offense must be alleged in the information so the accused can prepare her defense, and the nature of the charge is determined by the facts recited in it (canceran v. people; domingo v. rayala). the rule that corporate officers who participate in a corporate violation are criminally liable (people v. tan boon kong; sia v. people) applies only where the information charged them in that capacity.

the defect is not cured by documents attached to the information, such as affidavits, a boarding certificate, or receipts, that identify the accused as owner or officer. that the attachments point to different capacities only highlights the defect in the charge.

atty. riza s. fernandez, petitioner, vs. willie fernando maaliw, respondent. xi. law on public officers > d. accountability of public officers (ra 6713) > 2. discipline **a decision of the civil service commission dismissing an administrative complaint for lack of a prima facie case is appealable to the court of appeals by petition for review under rule 43**, consistent with section 9(3) of bp 129 and section 73, rule 13 of the rraccs. the non-appealability rules invoked do not apply: section 47, book v, title i of the administrative code of 1987 covers decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine not exceeding 30 days' salary, and section 72 of the rraccs covers decisions of agencies that would otherwise be appealable to the csc.

**the private complainant may appeal the csc decision in appropriate cases.** the rraccs provisions on elevating decisions of the csc and its regional offices use the generic term "party" (or "either by the complainant or the respondent"), not "party adversely affected," which the rraccs uses only for motions for reconsideration in disciplinary cases and appeals in non-disciplinary cases. the *mendez v. csc* line limiting appeals to the party adversely affected was overruled in *csc v. dacoycoy*, and *pnb v. garcia* and *constantino-david v. pangandaman-gania* recognized the private complainant's standing.

01-rosario-ponencias/gr-216723-20220309:
republic of the philippines, represented by the department of public works and highways (dpwh), petitioner, vs. pacita villao and carmienett javier, respondents. v. special civil actions > g. expropriation (rule 67; ra 10752, as amended by ra 12289) > 3. just compensation just compensation is the full and fair equivalent of the property taken; "[t]he measure is not the taker's gain, but the owner's loss" (const., art. iii, sec. 9). under **rule 67, section 4**, it is determined **as of the date of the taking or of the filing of the complaint, whichever came first**. if there was no actual taking before suit, it is reckoned from the filing of the **original** complaint, not a later amended complaint (reiterated).

the court may consider the standards in **section 5 of ra 8974** (the law when the case began; since repealed by ra 10752), including the current selling price of similar lands in the vicinity. but the evidence must show the property's value **as of the reckoning date**. **a commissioners' report has no sufficient legal basis if it simply adopts the per-square-meter valuation fixed in another expropriation case (whose decision does not show when that complaint was filed or the taking occurred) and relies on undated "current market offerings."** the remedy is to remand for a proper determination (following *npc v. diato-bernal* and *npc v. ycla sugar development corp.*).

legal interest on the **unpaid balance** (just compensation less the initial deposit) runs **from the issuance of the writ of possession**, when the deprivation of property can be established (*republic v. macabagdal*). the rates are:

municipality of makati (now city of makati), petitioner, vs. municipality of taguig (now city of taguig), respondent. xiii. local governments > d. powers and administration of local government units (lgu) > 4. settlement of boundary disputes creating lgus and fixing their boundaries is a legislative function, so in a boundary dispute the court only **carries legislative intent into effect**. the charters come first. where the charters do not state the territory in metes and bounds and only adopt historical boundaries (as with makati and taguig), the court weighs **historical evidence, maps, cadastral surveys, and the contemporaneous acts of lawful authorities**. it may take judicial notice of official acts of the three branches (rule 129, sec. 1). the plaintiff lgu must prove by **preponderance of evidence** that its claim aligns more with legislative intent. the plebiscite requirement first appeared in the 1973 constitution and applies only prospectively (ceniza). so the pre-1973 laws and proclamations of the bodies that then controlled boundaries carry great weight. census results, comelec certifications of voting since 1975, and similar documents do not fix boundaries.

applying by analogy the public international law concept of the **critical date** (when the dispute crystallized), the court gave little to no probative value to acts done after that date to improve a party's position, unless they were a normal continuation of earlier acts. here the critical date was january 31, 1990 (proclamation no. 518), so makati's 1994 cadastral survey had scarce probative value. **fort bonifacio (parcels 3 and 4, psu-2031), including the embo and inner fort barangays, belongs to taguig.**

01-rosario-ponencias/gr-236956-20211124:
department of finance-revenue integrity protection service (dof-rips), represented by joel m. apolonio and agapito c. guarin, petitioner, vs. office of the ombudsman and ramir saunders gomez, special agent i, bureau of customs, respondents. ii. the revised penal code – book one > d. extinction of criminal liability > 1. total extinction > e. prescription > ii. prescription under special laws (act 3326) **section 8 of ra 6713 amended section 7 of ra 3019 on the non-filing of the saln, through the express repealing clause in section 16 of ra 6713.** section 16 repeals or modifies inconsistent laws "unless the same provide for a heavier penalty." ra 6713 imposes the heavier penalty: imprisonment not exceeding five years, a fine not exceeding p5,000, or both, plus disqualification from public office. ra 3019 imposes only a fine of p100 to p1,000, imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. because the repeal is express, the rule against implied repeals does not apply. **a public officer cannot be indicted for the same non-filing under both laws; he may be prosecuted only under ra 6713.**

ra 6713 sets no prescriptive period, so act no. 3326 governs. **a violation of section 8 of ra 6713 prescribes in eight years** (act no. 3326, sec. 1(c): imprisonment of two years or more but less than six years). the 15-year period for ra 3019 offenses under bp 195 does not apply. this reiterates del rosario v. people, dof-rips v. ombudsman (casayuran), and dof-rips v. ombudsman (germar).

**perjury (art. 183, rpc) committed through false statements in a saln prescribes in ten years (art. 90), reckoned from the filing of the saln**, not from the complainant's later discovery of the falsity (reiterating germar). perjury is consummated upon filing, and the saln is then open to review. this harmonizes article 91 of the rpc with section 8(c)(4) of ra 6713, which keeps salns available to the public for ten years. the court applied the same reckoning to the falsification charges based on the same saln entries. the court also reiterated that it does not interfere with the ombudsman's investigatory and prosecutorial findings unless grave abuse of discretion is shown; mere disagreement is not enough. xi. law on public officers > d. accountability of public officers (ra 6713) > 4. the ombudsman and the special prosecutor (ra 6770) > d. judicial review
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-228607-20211005:
reynaldo a. bodo, petitioner, vs. commission on audit, respondent. vii. constitutional commissions > b. civil service commission (csc), commission on elections (comelec), and commission on audit (coa) > 2. powers, functions, and jurisdiction all government officers directly responsible for an unlawful expenditure may be held civilly liable to return the disallowed amount, from those who authorized or made the illegal payment **to those who merely took part in or contributed to it**. **but liability attaches only upon a showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence** (section 43, book vi, in relation to sections 38 and 39, book i, 1987 administrative code; rules 2a and 2b of the *madera* rules on return). applying these rules, the court held that **a requisitioning officer who signs the purchase request may be held solidarily liable for a disallowed procurement.** a purchase request is "not a mere mechanical act." under section 359 of the local government code, the head of the office needing the supplies must prepare it, certify that the supplies are necessary for official use, and specify the project where they will be used. the goods must be described technically, without brand names (r.a. no. 9184, section 18). the request is one of the documents that set procurement in motion. gross negligence or bad faith was shown here because the officer signed the request after the mayor had already approved it, and the request named a brand supplied exclusively by one contractor.

**the solidary liability under section 43 does not necessarily equal the full disallowed amount.** when the disallowance arises from an unlawful or irregular government contract and the government received and used the goods, the liability may be reduced under the principle of *quantum meruit* (guideline 2c of *torreta v. coa*). the contractor may keep the reasonable value of its deliveries, and that value is deducted from the disallowed amount. fixing the quantity delivered and a fair unit price is a factual, technical matter for the coa. the reduction also benefits solidary co-debtors who did not join the petition, because their liabilities are so closely related that one cannot be fixed without affecting the other. the court applied *madera* and *torreta*; it did not lay down a new rule. v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64)
01-rosario-ponencias/gr-235764-20210914:
rafael m. crisol, jr., petitioner, vs. commission on audit, respondent. xi. law on public officers > d. accountability of public officers (ra 6713) > 1. forms of accountability **a superior public officer cannot be held civilly liable for a subordinate's unremitted collections without a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence.** under section 38, chapter 9, book i of the administrative code of 1987, a public officer is not civilly liable for acts done in the performance of official duties unless there is a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence. a superior officer is not civilly liable for the wrongful acts, omissions, negligence or misfeasance of subordinates unless he actually authorized by written order the specific act or misconduct complained of. under sections 16.1 and 16.2 of the 2009 rules and regulations on the settlement of accounts (rrsa), liability for audit charges is measured by each officer's duties and individual participation in the charged transaction.

**gross negligence** is the want of even slight care: acting or failing to act where there is a duty to act, "not inadvertently but willfully and intentionally with a conscious indifference to consequences." for public officials, it is a breach of duty that is flagrant and palpable. it must be proved by evidence and **cannot be inferred from speculation** that a subordinate's failure to remit resulted from the superior's failure to monitor or remind him. a coa finding of ordinary negligence (failure to observe the diligence of a good father of a family) is not enough.

payment of the charge by the principal obligor extinguishes the solidary obligation (civil code, art. 1217), but the case is not moot while other issues remain, such as the finding of liability itself and the referral to the ombudsman. the court may relax the rules on finality in its equity jurisdiction when the merits and special circumstances warrant (applied). v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64) viii. obligations and contracts > a. obligations > 3. civil obligations > e. joint and solidary

social security system, petitioner, vs. commission on audit, respondent. vii. constitutional commissions > b. civil service commission (csc), commission on elections (comelec), and commission on audit (coa) > 2. powers, functions, and jurisdiction **goccs like the sss are always subject to the president's supervision and control. a charter power to fix reasonable compensation, allowances and benefits, plus an exemption from the salary standardization law, does not excuse a gocc from securing the president's approval, through the dbm, before granting allowances and benefits** (p.d. no. 1597, secs. 5 and 6; m.o. no. 20, s. 2001; j.r. no. 4; e.o. no. 7, s. 2010). the court reiterated *sss v. coa*, g.r. no. 243278, november 3, 2020. allowances paid beyond the dbm-approved corporate operating budget and without presidential approval are properly disallowed.

on liability, **the approving and certifying officers were absolved from solidary liability on account of good faith**, because no ruling then specifically required presidential approval for the sss. **every recipient, however, whether an approving or certifying officer or a mere passive recipient, must individually return what he or she received** under the madera rules on return (*madera v. coa*, as clarified by *abellanosa v. coa*), since the benefits had no legal basis. passive payees are excused only in special situations, as in the 2020 *sss* case, where the coa proper had excused them and the issue was not raised on review, so that ruling became final.

the court also clarified two procedural rules "for purposes of guiding the bar":
- *filing by registered mail.* the date of mailing is the date of filing (sec. 3, rule ix, 2009 revised rules of procedure of the coa; cf. sec. 3, rule 13, rules of court). the party asserting a mailing date must prove the fact and the date of mailing. where the registry receipts and envelope are missing, the court may weigh the surrounding circumstances, and a coa "received" stamp alone does not show personal filing.
- *notice to counsel.* when a party is represented by counsel, the period runs from receipt by counsel. the coa rules do not provide how a regional director's decision is served on a represented party, so the rules of court apply. a gocc legal department structured like a law firm is the counsel, and receipt by any of its divisions is receipt by counsel even if the handling lawyer gets the document later.

the court nevertheless relaxed the 180-day period in the interest of substantial justice, because the delay was short and showed no intent to delay. v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64) iii. civil procedure > e. pleadings > 10. filing and service (rules 13 and 13-a, as amended; am 10-3-7-sc, 11-9-4-sc, 25-01-13-sc, and 25-09-16-sc)

saripoden ariman guro, petitioner, vs. commission on elections and somerado malomalo guro, respondents. xii. election law > e. remedies and jurisdiction > 1. petition to deny due course or cancel certificate of candidacy a petition that seeks to disqualify a candidate on the ground of **ineligibility** (here, that he is not a registered voter of the municipality) is in the nature of a **petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy under section 78 of the omnibus election code**, whatever its caption. it must be filed within the period in rule 23, section 2 of the comelec rules of procedure (as amended by comelec resolution no. 9523): within five days from the last day for filing cocs, but **not later than 25 days from the filing of the coc** being challenged.

where the alleged ineligibility is misrepresentation as to being a registered voter, the period is **applied strictly**, as with age or residence. the court relaxes it only in exceptional situations, such as the lack of philippine citizenship (aznar; frivaldo), a supervening event that supplies the ground (hayudini), or peculiar circumstances showing diligence (caballero; ocate). dismissing a late petition on this ground is not grave abuse of discretion. v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64)

social security system (sss), petitioner, vs. commission on audit (coa), respondent. vii. constitutional commissions > b. civil service commission (csc), commission on elections (comelec), and commission on audit (coa) > 2. powers, functions, and jurisdiction **a rule 64 petition against a coa decision must be filed within 30 days from notice. a motion for reconsideration only interrupts the period; if it is denied, the petitioner has only the remaining period, but not less than five days, from notice of the denial** (rule 64, section 3). a petition filed beyond that period leaves the coa decision final and executory. the notice issued by the commission secretary in the form prescribed by coa resolution no. 2013-018 (amending section 12, rule x of the 2009 revised rules of procedure of the coa) validly communicates the commission proper's denial of the motion, and the remaining period runs from its receipt, not from a later coa letter answering a request for the minutes.

reiterated: **only rank-and-file employees who are members of the collective negotiating unit are entitled to cna incentives; high-level managerial and confidential employees (including coterminous and highly confidential employees, lawyers and executives) are not**, because they cannot become members of the negotiating unit. their contribution to agency efficiency is immaterial (pd 1597, section 5; eo 180, section 3; ao 103, s. 2004, section 3(b); pslmc resolution no. 4, s. 2002 and no. 2, s. 2003; ao 135, section 2; dbm budget circular no. 2006-1, section 4.2). a predetermined fixed cna incentive also violates section 5.6 of dbm budget circular no. 2006-1.

applying *madera v. coa* and *sss v. coa* (2020): **the presumption of good faith of approving and certifying officers fails when an explicit law, rule or regulation has been violated**, so they must return the disallowed amounts; **the recipient employees must return what they received on the ground of solutio indebiti.** v. special civil actions > d. review of commission on elections and commission on audit judgments and final orders or resolutions (rule 64) v. labor relations > a. right to self-organization > 1. coverage > a. government employees x. quasi-contracts > b. kinds > 2. solutio indebiti
